headline: Communist Party of India State secretary M. Veerapandian made a strong case for abolishing the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), arguing that it was not only an assault on social justice, but had also created an atmosphere of fear and an...
full_text:
Communist Party of India State secretary M. Veerapandian made a strong case for abolishing the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), arguing that it was not only an assault on social justice, but had also created an atmosphere of fear and anxiety among students aspiring to pursue medical education.
He said education — both school and higher education — was the responsibility of a welfare state and should not be left in the hands of private institutions. “Education is not a privilege or a concession; it is a right. The government must take responsibility for providing education, just as China, a country with a population comparable to India’s, provides education to its citizens,” Mr. Veerapandian said.
As Balan Illam, the CPI headquarters, has emerged as a centre for protests against NEET, Mr. Veerapandian said the party had permitted students to stage demonstrations following requests from the All India Students’ Federation (AISF) and students affiliated with the Cockroach Janta Party. “We also took into account the convenience of our students staying at Balan Illam and neighbours on the road. We were convinced that peaceful demonstrations would not cause any disruption,” he said.
‘Complete exemption’
With reference to the celebration following the resignation of the Union Higher Education Minister, Mr. Veerapandian said that, as far as Tamil Nadu was concerned, the demand was for complete exemption from the examination.
“If other States wish to continue with NEET, we have no objection. The students’ demand for the Minister’s resignation over the alleged question paper leak is also justified. The government should hold talks with them. Suppressing peaceful protests through police action is an assault on democratic values and the Gandhian tradition of peaceful protest,” he said.
Reiterating that NEET was not an appropriate method for admitting students to medical colleges, Mr. Veerapandian recalled the views of the late neurologist B. Ramamurthi, who had argued that medical education did not depend solely on rote learning or examination scores.
Mr. Veerapandian said government-run institutions such as Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital and Stanley Medical College Hospital could match any world-class hospital. He pointed out that these institutions had treated and saved more than one lakh patients during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“We have doctors of exceptional talent and skill who may not have entered medical colleges through NEET. We need a serious debate on the examination. On the one hand, it is an assault on social justice; on the other, it creates an atmosphere of fear and anxiety among students aspiring to study medicine,” he said.
Referring to Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay’s opposition to NEET, Mr. Veerapandian said the Chief Minister should remain steadfast in his stand. “His recent statement suggests that he is firm in his opposition,” he added.
He also urged the government to earmark designated venues where public protests could be held in the State in future. “Peaceful protests strengthen democracy; they are not directed against governments, The government should facilitate such democratic expression rather than suppress it.” he said.

headline: Former J&K Chief Minister and Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) president Mehbooba Mufti on Saturday (July 25, 2026) congratulated the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) for its “success” and said it has managed to “reclaim Mahatma Gandhi’s idea of India”.
full_text:
Former J&K Chief Minister and Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) president Mehbooba Mufti on Saturday (July 25, 2026) congratulated the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) for its “success” and said it has managed to “reclaim Mahatma Gandhi’s idea of India”.
“For more than a month, these youths were out without food. They adopted a Gandhian style. The biggest success is that these youths reclaimed Gandhi’s idea of India. They have rejected and dismissed divisive politics, especially Hindu-Muslim politics. It has given hope, otherwise amid a sense of dejection. It seems the future of India is in safe hands,” said Ms. Mufti.
She praised the CJP for allowing her to speak at the Jantar Mantar recently and backed its demands for compensation to the families of students who ended their lives and an apology for the atrocities allegedly committed on the youth by the Delhi police.
“We were warmly welcomed despite the narrative of Kashmiris being separatists and anti-nationals. It was heartening to see that this generation puts more focus on the future of the country than the Hindu-Muslim divide. I am hopeful what J&K students faced outside will also stop now,” said Ms. Mufti.
She said what started in Kashmir is now reaching every corner of India. “Peaceful protests silenced with lathis. Constitutional promises broken. Institutions weakened. Today, minority rights are under threat. Tomorrow, no citizen’s voice or vote will matter. The unity seen at Jantar Mantar is the real backbone of this nation. This isn’t just a struggle for one community; it is a fight to save humanity, democracy, and the soul of India,” said Ms. Mufti.
Ms. Mufti also raised the issue of Muslim women, saying these women were facing “harassment for wearing a burqa or hijab.“ You cannot praise Islamic heritage and culture on visits abroad while turning a blind eye to the harassment of Muslim women at home. True empowerment isn’t a slogan for foreign trips. It is guaranteeing safety, dignity, and religious freedom for every woman in India,” she added.

headline: Outside the imposing gate of the sprawling Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, Mohd. Waseem, a carpenter, has forfeited a day’s wages to support students protesting against a district administration notice.
full_text:
Outside the imposing gate of the sprawling Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, Mohd. Waseem, a carpenter, has forfeited a day’s wages to support students protesting against a district administration notice.
The sit-in protest began on July 18 after the Rampur Development Authority (RDA) issued an order to demolish 38 of the 40 buildings on the campus, alleging that they had been built without approved construction plans.
The move marks a major escalation after years of State scrutiny over alleged illegal land acquisition and lease violations.
Holding a placard that places “ilm” (learning) above all else, the school dropout says he shares an emotional connection with the institution because he contributed to its woodwork. “I am here to appeal for the university to be saved. Otherwise, I fear the youngsters of the region will have to work as labourers like me.”
Braving the heat and humidity, around 100 university students are huddled under a plastic tent a few metres away, raising slogans against the district administration, holding portraits of B.R. Ambedkar in their laps and copies of the Constitution in their hands. “No one is leading this protest. It is a question of our career and safety. Our parents believe in this university,” says Iqra, a law student at the university, who rushed from her home in Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, when the news broke. “It seems the administration has succumbed to the interests of its political masters, but our protest is anything but political,” she says.
While the university administration strongly disputes the legality of the demolition order and has approached the Moradabad Divisional Commissioner for redress, anxious students find themselves caught in the crossfire between administrative enforcement and what they describe as “political targeting”. “It seems the government wants to tell us that Azam Khan committed a crime by building a temple of education for us and that we have sinned by taking admission to it,” says Saqib Sayeed, a postgraduate law student and a practising lawyer whose voice has turned hoarse from constant sloganeering.
Set in stone
Established in 2006 through an Act of the State Legislature by the Maulana Mohammad Ali Jauhar Trust under the leadership of Samajwadi Party (SP) founding member Azam Khan, the university’s 250-acre campus provides higher education in diverse disciplines, including engineering, pharmacy, law and agriculture, to over 2,400 students.
It is recognised by the University Grants Commission (UGC) and was granted minority status in 2014 after then Governor Aziz Qureshi assented to the Bill, seven years after the State Assembly passed it.
At present, Khan and his son, Abdullah Azam Khan, are serving prison sentences following multiple convictions, including in a forgery case involving duplicate Permanent Account Number (PAN) cards.
The Rampur district court also upheld an additional two-year prison sentence against Khan for violating the Model Code of Conduct during the 2019 Lok Sabha election campaign. During the campaign, he made derogatory “shoe-cleaning” remarks about the then District Magistrate Aunjaneya Kumar Singh, who now serves as the Moradabad Divisional Commissioner. The ball is now in his court.
In January, Khan resigned as the chairperson of the trust, passing the baton to his sister, Nikhat Aflaq, and his eldest son, Adeeb Azam. He continues to serve as the university’s Chancellor. People in his inner circle say the move was intended to safeguard the university’s interests from what they describe as “political vendetta” against him.
Invoking Section 27(1) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, in his order, District Magistrate Ajay Kumar Dwivedi, who is also the Vice-Chairman of the RDA, noted that only the university’s medical college building and one academic block had valid construction approvals obtained from the district panchayat.
The administration maintained that because the management had previously secured approvals for those two buildings, it was fully aware of the legal requirements governing the remaining 38 structures.
Sources say the move stemmed from the 2023 Income Tax raid, which pointed to discrepancies in valuation and alleged underreporting of the cost of the structures, including two mosques.
The university’s principal argument is that most of the campus was constructed before 2016. At that time, the area where the university is located did not fall under the RDA watch. It contends that the university came under the authority’s jurisdiction only in 2024. Therefore, it argues, the RDA’s regulations cannot be applied retrospectively. Advocate Kashif Sarvat, a member of the university’s legal team, says they presented no-objection certificates issued by the then Gram Panchayat for the buildings, which, like those of any educational institution, were constructed over time. However, he says, the District Magistrate decided to proceed with the demolition order.
False impression
The students allege that the district administration is trying to hollow out the university by creating panic among them. “A day after the notice, a camp was organised just outside the gate where district officials, along with agents and faculty members from a government college and an upcoming private university in Moradabad, tried to terrorise students about their future by creating a false narrative that the university was going to be demolished soon,” says Sayeed, wondering how the buildings could be illegal if the UGC recognised the university’s degrees. “Even if they are, a penalty can be imposed.”
Azra Fatima, who enrolled in the Bachelor of Education programme after completing a B.Sc. in Zoology, says she has devoted five years to the university because she has faith in its faculty and academic environment. “We have empathy for the students sitting at Jantar Mantar because their struggle is also about education, but right now our focus is on saving our campus.”
It was only after Vice-Chancellor Prof. Zaheeruddin sent a notice to the District Magistrate, invoking an Allahabad High Court order of 2019, that the camp was removed two days later. “I can’t comment on the details because the matter is sub judice, but we have a strong legal basis. An appeal has been filed before the Commissioner’s court. Further, we can invoke Article 226 before the High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court,” says Prof. Zaheeruddin, adding that the law itself recognises that certain construction-related violations may be addressed through regularisation, compounding or post facto approval.
“Why can’t the powers that be respect a centre of education that serves students from all communities in Rampur?” the Vice-Chancellor says. A senior professor of law at Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) before joining the university after his retirement, he claims: “Every year, the administration tries to create the impression that the university is on the verge of closure to drive students away, perhaps creating a situation where it is reduced to a structure that can be bulldozed under some regulation. If push comes to shove, we will teach students on the road.”
A centre of education and Islamic learning, Rampur is remembered as the birthplace of Mohammed Ali Jauhar, the freedom fighter and journalist who co-founded the Khilafat Movement and Jamia Millia Islamia in Delhi. He served as president of the Indian National Congress in 1923. Jauhar also held the rare distinction of serving as president of the All-India Muslim League. After the Non-Cooperation Movement and the publication of the Nehru Report, he distanced himself from the Congress. Though Jauhar died in 1931, long before the demand for a separate Muslim State crystallised, his association with the League gives right-wing elements fodder to question Khan’s decision to name the university after Rampur’s most celebrated son.
Contrasting image
Rampur, the Lok Sabha constituency once represented by India’s first Education Minister Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, was home to institutions such as the Raza Library and Madarsa Aliya, which attracted researchers from across the world. Over the years, the city has lost much of its educational and cultural sheen due to a combination of geopolitical shifts, economic stagnation and political polarisation. Today, the nearest government university is in Bareilly, about 70 km away.
Khan’s supporters say he sought to restore the city’s lost glory by building a university on the lines of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan’s vision for AMU, catering primarily to the underprivileged. Akseer Ahmad, a student with a disability who graduated from AMU, says he shifted to Jauhar University because it offers greater fee concessions to Persons with Disabilities (PwD) than other institutions.
Usman Ali, an engineering student, says he availed himself of the quota for wards of single mothers. Female students speak of the safe and affordable bus and rickshaw services provided by the university. “In the city of knives, Azam Khan has placed a pen in the hands of the poor, but it seems the government wants to snatch it away,” says Angel Bharti, a Class 12 student who hopes to pursue undergraduate studies at the university.
Khan’s detractors, however, point to the criminal investigation and court case involving the alleged theft of thousands of rare books, ancient manuscripts and antique furniture from the 250-year-old Madarsa Aliya, which investigators claim were recovered from the university’s central Mumtaz Library, modelled on the U.S. Capitol Building. The protest has once again brought into focus the university’s grand buildings, inspired by architectural landmarks from around the world.
The Rabindranath Tagore Auditorium incorporates elements of classical Greek architecture, while the administrative block is reminiscent of Hyderabad’s Falaknuma Palace.
The seven-storey water tank has an elevator leading to a serene artificial lake beside the Kosi riverbed. A replica of the Ashoka Pillar stands in the central courtyard facing the mosque, creating a striking visual axis. Positioned prominently beside this axis is a decommissioned Soviet-era T-55 battle tank.
From allegations of using enemy property to charges of forcibly acquiring farmers’ land and non-payment of labour cess, the university has for years faced administrative and legal action arising from multiple State government investigations. However, the latest demolition notice has softened the stance of even some of Khan’s fiercest critics. The common refrain is that even if government funds were misused to build a private university, the money was ultimately public. “Demolition is no solution,” says Mohd. Danish, an advocate, pointing out that even the administration converted the university’s medical college into a COVID-19 facility during the pandemic.
Fasahat Ali Khan Shanu, once a close associate of Khan and now a Muslim face of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), says just as no one can erase Madan Mohan Malaviya’s contribution to Banaras Hindu University, no one can take away Khan’s role in establishing the university. However, he adds, “It is time the government takes it over.”
He has submitted a memorandum to the Commissioner to this effect.
However, as it is a minority institution, stakeholders acknowledge that taking it over would require a substantial legislative exercise.
Political fallout
As delegations from Opposition parties and social organisations flock to the campus in support of the students, the issue is increasingly taking on a political colour a year ahead of the Assembly election, generating sympathy for Khan. Asim Raja, Khan’s chief election agent and media in-charge, who oversees organisational work in his absence, sees the demolition notice as yet another attempt by the State government to “divert attention” from its failures and polarise the electorate.
He admits that the protest has helped paper over the cracks within SP. The party’s Rampur MP, Mohibullah Nadvi, whose candidature was pushed through by party president Akhilesh Yadav despite Khan’s reservations, has also come out in support of the university.
Awdhesh Sharma, a grassroots BJP worker, says the city stands with the students and their future, but there is no love lost for Khan.
“We all know the kind of influence and pressure he used to build his dream project and how it has remained mired in controversies. The issue might strengthen the SP’s vote bank, but it is not going to pay dividends beyond Rampur.”
Political observers and senior bureaucrats believe that the ruling party stands to gain more from the developments. There is a perception that even if Khan has lost some of his political heft, a large section of Muslim youth, not just in Rampur but across Uttar Pradesh, still sees him as a defender of minority identity and a counterweight to the Hindutva onslaught.
“Azam Khan’s name helps the BJP polarise elections in at least 150 constituencies across Uttar Pradesh. It appears that keeping his spectre alive in a Muslim-majority constituency is not a bad bargain. His resurgence in the run-up to State polls is more of a headache for Akhilesh Yadav, as the seasoned politician is known to bargain hard with the party president for seats,” says a senior bureaucrat, requesting anonymity.
When he was out on bail in 2025, a party insider says, his proximity to Azad Samaj Party leader Chandrashekhar Azad Ravan created a major political buzz, sending the SP leadership into a tizzy. There are whispers at the protest site about whether Akhilesh, who has largely maintained a strategic distance from what are seen as “Muslim issues”, will raise concerns over the proposed demolition of Khan’s pride and joy with the same vigour that he displayed over the paper leak issue. For now, to quell speculation, a high-level party delegation led by Mata Prasad Pandey, Leader of the Opposition in the State Assembly, has met the District Magistrate.
Personal battle?
Those tracking Khan’s legal trajectory under the current administration will recognise that Commissioner Singh has been the central administrative figure behind the legal and regulatory action against Khan’s political and institutional empire.
The Sikkim-cadre IAS officer joined the Uttar Pradesh cadre on inter-cadre deputation in 2015, when the SP government was in power in the State. Owing to successive extensions granted by the Central government at the request of the Uttar Pradesh government, his deputation has stretched into an unprecedented 11-year tenure in his home State. With his current tenure officially ending on August 14, a section of people in Rampur links the recent developments to his future. Singh rejects the suggestion, saying the demolition order reflected the District Magistrate’s assessment. “He felt compounding was not possible because the entire layout had not been approved. I know that health and education are of paramount importance. Within the framework of the law, we need to find a way out,” says Singh.

headline: CHANDIGARH: Twenty-seven years after leading the Army during the 1999
full_text:
CHANDIGARH: Twenty-seven years after leading the Army during the 1999 
Kargil War, former Army chief General VP Malik (retd) said the conflict's hard lessons - from equipment shortages and intelligence gaps to the need for self-reliance - transformed India's military capabilities, enabling the precision strikes on Pakistani airfields during last year's 
Operation Sindoor without crossing the border.
"The biggest operational lessons were the need to strengthen intelligence, surveillance and achieve 'atmanirbharta (self-reliance)' in military hardware," Gen Malik told TOI in an interview ahead of the 27th anniversary of 
Kargil Vijay Diwas. Those lessons, he said, shaped India's military preparedness over the next two decades.
Citing Operation Sindoor, he pointed to the armed forces' growing reliance on short- and long-range drones for surveillance and precision strikes, along with advanced rockets and missiles. 
CJP Jantar Mantar Protest Updates
"We did not have to enter Pakistani territory when we struck airfields and radar stations, causing major havoc," he said, contrasting it with Kargil.
He said indigenous and imported platforms, including BrahMos, Akash and the S-400, were now tested in real-world conditions. Combined with an integrated tri-services command under Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), they have significantly strengthened India's defence capability.
Yet, Gen Malik stressed that technology alone could not win wars. "The man behind the gun is always more important. We must look after them," he said.
Recalling his visits to the frontlines in Jammu & Kashmir, Gen Malik said the soldiers themselves became a source of strength. "...every six days, I would visit... While morale in Delhi was sometimes anxious or uncertain, not a single soldier ever told me the task was difficult. Every visit replenished my own morale."
Reflecting on the reforms that followed the war, Gen Malik said govt constituted Kargil Review Committee, whose key recommendations included creating the CDS position to improve tri-service integration and civil-military coordination. He added that commemorating Vijay Diwas was not only about paying homage to the martyrs but also ensuring the lessons of the conflict continued to guide armed forces.
Gen Malik said the valour displayed remained an inspiration for future generations. While the victory involved strategic planning at the highest level, he insisted the credit belonged to the young officers and soldiers who fought at unforgiving heights. "We must also remember the supporting arms and services. People often forget them but military functions like an orchestra during war. When every arm works in harmony, we achieve victory."
Invoking Bhagavad Gita, he said, "The true test of any plan lies in its execution. As written in the Gita: 'Action is superior to knowledge'."

headline: With Haryana completing the first phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) across the State, the names of 33,84,568 electors went unrecorded as a result of permanent relocation, absence, death or duplicate entries.
full_text:
With Haryana completing the first phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) across the State, the names of 33,84,568 electors went unrecorded as a result of permanent relocation, absence, death or duplicate entries.
Haryana’s Chief Electoral Officer A. Sreenivas said that the first phase of the SIR in the State has been completed and the draft electoral roll will be published on July 31, which will be made available on the official website as well as at all designated publication centres.
Addressing a press conference here, Mr. Sreenivas said that 20,629 Booth Level Officers (BLOs) distributed enumeration forms to more than 2 crore electors, out of which over 1 crore enumeration forms have been digitised.
“However, the names of 33,84,568 electors could not be recorded. Of these, 13,75,278 had permanently shifted, 7,66,205 were found to be deceased, 2,04,916 were already registered as electors, 9,36,646 electors were found absent, while 1,01,523 electors did not submit their enumeration forms due to other reasons,” he said.
He said that claims and objections can be filed from July 31 to August 30. “If the name of any elector does not appear in the draft electoral roll to be published on July 31, he or she may submit Form 6 to get the name included again. The name will be included in the final electoral roll,” he said.
“The name of any elector will not be deleted without giving an opportunity of hearing. If an elector is aggrieved by the decision of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), an appeal may be filed before the District Magistrate within 15 days. If the grievance still persists, a further appeal may be filed before the Chief Electoral Officer within 30 days,” he added.
The final electoral roll will be published on October 3, he said. He said that 37,055 Booth Level Agents (BLAs) appointed by various political parties are also assisting in the process. “These include 19,051 appointed by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), 15,818 by the Indian National Congress, 1,476 by the Indian National Lok Dal (INLD), 54 by the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), 314 by the Communist Party of India (CPI) and 342 by the Jannayak Janata Party (JJP),” he said.

headline: New Delhi: A fiery speech by Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra during a debate in Lok Sabha on amendments to the anti-paper leak law set her on collision course with the Modi government Tuesday, after her comments aimed at newly appointed Union Educa...
full_text:
New Delhi: A fiery speech by Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra during a debate in Lok Sabha on amendments to the anti-paper leak law set her on collision course with the Modi government Tuesday, after her comments aimed at newly appointed Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi.
During the debate on The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, Priyanka also questioned the composition of the Nandan Nilekani-chaired high-powered task force on exam reforms constituted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Its members include, among others, former Intelligence Bureau (IB) chief Tapan Deka and IIT-Madras director V. Kamakoti, who Priyanka referred to as “an expert on gaumutra”.
The jibe was a reference to Kamakoti’s remarks in January 2025 about the “anti-bacterial” and “anti-fungal” properties of cow urine.
Other members of the panel include former ISRO chairman S. Somanath, former education secretary Anita Karwal, and former Bihar chief secretary Amrit Lal Meena.
Criticising Joshi’s appointment as education minister, Vadra remarked that the PM allocated the portfolio to a person who had defended the release of convicts in the Bilkis Bano case.
What message does that send to India’s girls, she asked.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju objected to the remark, saying it amounted to “character assassination within Parliament,” and asked that it be expunged and that Priyanka apologise to the House. Joshi, in turn, asked Vadra to authenticate her statement, and the Speaker told her not to make statements without facts, while BJP MP Nishikant Dubey said she should authenticate it first, and went on to make a remark about Jawaharlal Nehru’s personal life. Vadra said she would furnish evidence and authenticate it.
Joshi, along with Commerce Minister Piyush Goya and BJP MP Nishikant Dubey, later called on Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla over remarks made by Vadra in the House. Her remarks were later expunged from the record.
Joshi was given charge of the Education Ministry on 25 July after Dharmendra Pradhan under pressure from the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest. In 2022, as Parliamentary Affairs Minister, Joshi had defended the release of the 11 men convicted of gang-raping Bilkis Bano, who was five-months pregnant at the time, and killing seven of her family during the 2002 Gujarat riots, saying he found nothing wrong as the remission was granted in accordance with the due process of law.
Speaking to reporters outside Parliament after the debate, Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi carried the charge further. He said the BJP had made “a defender of rapists” the education minister. “There can be no filthier man than somebody who says that rapists need protection,” he said, adding that the Prime Minister could have chosen anyone from his Cabinet but picked a “person who protects rapists”.
On the Bill itself, Vadra said its main change was to increase the punishment for paper leaks, but that no offender had been punished since the parent Act was passed in 2024.
She said the names and addresses of students who took part in the recent protests were being made public through facial recognition technology, while no such action was taken against those behind paper leaks, and that the Bill had no concrete measures to prevent leaks.
She said the Prime Minister needed to change his advisers, who she said were disconnected from reality, and that new committees would not solve the problem, noting that the recommendations of the earlier Radhakrishna Committee had not been implemented.
The committee was set up under former ISRO chief K. Radhakrishnan to reform the NTA after the 2024 NEET-UG paper leak.
Vadra also contrasted the welcome given to Pradhan at Makar Dwar of Parliament with a death in Maharashtra, where a family was mourning a daughter who died by suicide after being affected by a paper leak.
She said that where there should have been shame, there was celebration.
The Congress MP went further to add that the examination system had failed, citing 152 paper leaks over the last decade affecting 7.5 crore students, with no culprit or paper-leak mafia punished. She said the government had hollowed out the education system by stacking it with RSS pracharaks, had set up the NTA and centralised the system, and that the share of education in the Union budget was declining.
On police action during the ‘Sansad Chalo’ protest march on 20 July, Vadra asked who had ordered the use of force. “What was the need to use pellet guns and AK-47s against the youth of this country? Were they terrorists?” she said, also citing use of tear gas, lathicharge and water cannons, and the treatment of young women by police personnel.
She asked whether the Prime Minister or Union Home Minister Amit Shah had given the order, and said the whole country, not the Congress alone, wanted an answer.
She also listed the protesters’ demands: action on the leaks, reform of the system, removal of paper leak mafias, the resignation of the minister during whose tenure the leaks occurred, action against those who used force against students, and an apology.
She said hundreds of students had died by suicide and others were in depression, and that families were taking loans and selling belongings to pay donations, capitation fees and coaching fees without any assurance of jobs.
Fast-track courts, she said, had a poor record, noting that the CBI counsel had not appeared at the first hearing of the fast-track court set up to hear paper leak cases, and, in a swipe at the Prime Minister, said that making videos from different camera angles would not win him the trust of India’s Gen Z.
Before her, allies of the government had defended it.
Shiv Sena MP Shrikant Eknath Shinde said no single exam could decide a student’s future and that the government stood with the youth, adding that it had not only condemned the paper leak but tried to clean the system, that Pradhan took onus, and that the NEET re-examination was held within 37 days and the result made public within 25 days.
TDP MP Lavu Sri Krishna Devarayalu proposed a national question bank and decentralised question-paper setting. He asked the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to fill vacancies in forensics to speed up investigations and, citing the 2012 Nirbhaya case, said the speed of fast-track courts needed monitoring, and called for coaching institutes to be made non-profit. When DMK MP Dayanidhi Maran called to ban NEET, Devarayalu said Tamil Nadu wanted to ban everything, which was why industries were moving to Andhra Pradesh.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

headline: Mumbai: Breaking ranks with aunt Supriya Sule, Rohit Pawar said Monday that the Delimitation Bills are a “dangerous proposition and not good for the country”. In an interview with ThePrint, the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) MLA fro...
full_text:
Mumbai: Breaking ranks with aunt Supriya Sule, Rohit Pawar said Monday that the Delimitation Bills are a “dangerous proposition and not good for the country”. In an interview with ThePrint, the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) MLA from Karjat-Jamkhed also ruled out the possibility of joining hands with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Rohit said enactment of The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 would allow redrawing of constituencies in a manner so as to benefit the BJP, which he cannot support.
“Whether it is done (by way of) 50 percent increase in seats uniformly across or more than that or less than that, according to me it is a dangerous proposition and not good for the country,” he told ThePrint.
Rohit’s aunt and NCP (SP) MP from Baramati, Supriya Sule, had last week told the media that her party may consider supporting the legislation if the government were to propose uniform increase of 50 percent in parliamentary seats across states. Her remarks were seen as an indication that the Sharad Pawar-led party may have softened its stance on the legislation, given that it had voted against The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026.
The proposed constitutional amendment was defeated in the Lok Sabha on 17 April, having failed to secure a two-thirds majority.
Speaking to ThePrint, Rohit Pawar said he had conveyed his opposition to the Delimitation Bills to leaders of his party. “There is democracy in our party and everyone holds their own views…but I also feel that what Supriya Sule said and meant was that the party would support it if it is done constitutionally, which I do not think the BJP will do.”
He cited delimitation in Assam in 2023 as an ‘example’ that such an exercise would benefit only the ruling BJP. According to an analysis by Frontline, the number of Muslim-dominated seats in the state “reduced from around 29–30 to 22–23, while Muslim-influenced seats dropped from 41 to 26” as a result of the exercise.
“The constituencies were redrawn such that it ended up helping the BJP only and I believe the same team is working on it on the national level.” Rohit Pawar said.
Speaking about the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) phenomenon, Rohit said the youth have given courage to opposition leaders who were on the fence regarding their support to the movement. “The youth have shown how to be fearless and they all came together irrespective of caste, creed or religion. They were all Indians and that renewed the energy within the Opposition camp,” he said. Adding, “Many leaders like Rahul Gandhi ji, (Sharad) Pawar saheb, Akhilesh ji have been speaking against the government but this movement has given leaders new hope and the Opposition camp is now going on the offensive.”
Also Read: Two birds with one merger—why BJP wants ‘united NCP’ in NDA fold
‘I definitely would not go with NDA’
During the interview, Rohit also stated in no uncertain terms that he was not in favour of the NCP(SP) joining the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA).
His remarks came against the backdrop of speculation that the NCP(SP) was considering joining hands with the BJP, though Supriya Sule had clarified earlier this month that her party was very much part of the INDIA bloc. The two NCP factions were in talks for a merger prior to Ajit Pawar’s death in a plane crash on 28 January.
Rohit Pawar, who has been vocal about his opposition to the NDA, said he prefers to stay in the Opposition rather than join hands with the BJP. “I am pretty clear that I want to stay in the Opposition and fight for people’s issues. I am 40-years-old and I have another 30 years in politics ahead of me. If all will join the NDA, who will stay in the Opposition?”
Adding, “I have been speaking to a lot of youngsters and students for the past few years. What I have realised is that they want a definite answer, yes or no. There should be no middle ground. So I definitely would not go with NDA.”
Rohit also called out leaders who believe in having a dialogue with the ruling BJP.
“Their intentions might be clean, they could be talking to ruling party leaders for constituency-related work or people’s issues,” he said. “But it creates a lot of confusion amongst the public. If you continuously and constantly meet ruling party members during work hours or after work, this will create confusion and people will stop believing in us.”
Without explicitly commenting on speculations about some leaders from NCP(SP) in favour of joining the NDA, Rohit said that if such an alliance were to happen, neither he nor Supriya Sule would be in favour of it. “If some leaders go to that side, I won’t even say bye to them. We will immediately start working and building our party,” he said.
Rohit Pawar also cited offers of ministerial berths as one of the reasons why many in the Opposition are considering switching to the ruling side. He claimed he was offered a ministerial berth many times in the past but turned it down.
When the Maha Vikas Aghadi (MVA) was in power, Rohit said he had the chance to become a minister because he is part of the Pawar clan, “but I did not”.
“Later, when Ajit dada broke away from the party, he offered me a post and asked me to join him. I refused. Then again after Lok Sabha and before Vidhan Sabha (elections), Ajit dada met me and offered a ministry to me. Again, I refused. So those who are going want to become ministers. I have already rejected that. So my ultimate goal is not to become the minister but to fight for the people. And so I will be aggressive against the BJP and NDA and stay in the Opposition,” he said.
The NCP(SP) MLA acknowledged that this decision puts him at risk since he is also has business interests but said he has already faced the Income Tax (IT) department and Enforcement Directorate (ED) and has nothing to hide.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

headline: New Delhi: Lok Sabha MP and BJP leader Kangana Ranaut continued her tirade against the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Wednesday, calling the CJP spokesperson Saurav Das “totally useless and unemployed”.
full_text:
New Delhi: Lok Sabha MP and BJP leader Kangana Ranaut continued her tirade against the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Wednesday, calling the CJP spokesperson Saurav Das “totally useless and unemployed”.
“Dear Saurav, your issues are personal, you are not a student, you are simply useless, let’s start with learning some skill. It’s a good place to start,” she posted on Instagram.
Kangana’s comments came shortly after Das came down heavily on her remarks on Gen Z protesters, especially women, and urged politicians to “uphold the dignity of their position”.
The Lok Sabha MP from Mandi in Himachal Pradesh said about the CJP spokesperson: “I googled this person and he is 28 years old, how he claims to be a student I have no clue!! Yes I am in politics for past two years but I have been in public life for last 20 years. At his age I had two national awards,” she said.
“Yes, as a new parliamentarian I was overwhelmed with all the work because I am also a filmmaker+performing artist+ producer+screen writer+entrepreneur. But some like him who are totally useless and unemployed will never understand what it means to be in massive demand at all times at any age,” she added.
The MP also attacked the media with this post: “The media is ganging up against me. And they won’t tell you how much I have praised startups like SkyRoot… our country’s Gen Z who are taking us to such heights… I myself congratulated NEET students. And those children, who take responsibility for their families… Just for a few followers, likes and comments the media has been sold out and some feminist anchors are doing a bulletin and teaching me that Kangana why should these women have the burden of dignity or discipline.”
Advising Gen Z, she added: “If it is related to my Gods, my leader PM Modi, you cannot abuse them… students call him exam buddy. Some call him leader, some, friend, family member and even God. You can’t hurt anyone’s feelings. This is not about acting cool. Don’t be impacted by Feminazi and don’t ruin your life. You have to stick to maryada when you go to your work place. Even science says the purpose of human lives is evolution and so do our shastras. But this Feminazi is teaching you to be animalistic… display animal tendencies… and go out of control and land in jail. You have to decide who is guiding you correctly.”
BJP national spokesperson R. P. Singh said that Kangana had made the comments in her personal capacity.
The controversy unfolded after the actor-politician shared a series of Instagram stories in which she referred to the young women participating in the CJP-led student protests at Jantar Mantar as ‘Generation Gutter‘.
Kangana also accused the protesters of glorifying “drugs, drinks and endless body counts”. The BJP MP had earlier also termed videos from the Jantar Mantar demonstrations as “puke-inducing”.
Her remarks came days after the 36-day agitation, spearheaded by the CJP at Jantar Mantar, ended on 25 July. In a post on Instagram on 27 July, Ranaut described videos of protesters at Jantar Mantar as display of “filth, garbage and ugliness”.
Das had dismissed Kangana’s criticism, saying: “Kangana Ranaut is not taken seriously by her own party. So why should we take her seriously? I don’t think anyone in Gen Z, or in Gen Alpha, or any younger generation takes her seriously. Or listens to her.”
Her comments were criticised by the Opposition, including the Congress and AIMIM, which demanded an apology from her.
Earlier, in yet another Instagram story, Kangana had also justified the crackdown by the Delhi Police. “Protesters who are getting beaten and abused on the roads by common people because of their filthy and abusive reels, they must understand, jab bolte ho toh sunna bhi padega (if you speak, be prepared to listen),” she said.
The Lok Sabha MP had further said that damaging public property and hurling abuses at the government would naturally provoke a response.
“If you damage public property, the public will damage you too. If you have a grievance with the country and its leadership and have publicly hurled vile abuses, then now you must listen to those who love this country and brought this government to power through the ballot,” she wrote in Hindi.
Even as Kangana continues her criticism of CJP and Gen Z, the BJP is trying to reach out to the younger generation. The party has been posting a number of videos on social media especially Instagram to reach out to them, many of which feature Gen Z and their issues, using words and phrases considered popular among young users.
One such video, posted by the BJP from its national handle on X shows a conversation among youth and trainers at a gym.
After being pointed out by young people that the current generation prefers to ‘look ahead’ rather than dwell on history, one of the trainers responds: “India of the past… scams, blasts, and instability. India of today… smartphones in hand, metros, expressways, new airports, and the rapid expansion of IITs, IIMs, and AIIMS. Development that stalled for decades is now surging ahead at a rapid pace. As the nation advances under strong leadership, seize this opportunity and focus on your career,” says an another gym trainer to a number of youngsters while explaining why young people should draw inspiration from India’s past.
“And by the way… someone’s resignation is not a personal victory for any single individual, but a symbol of the strength of democracy. The government is continuously working to address challenges and build a better future for the youth. Stay focused on your future… because a strong India = a stronger future.”
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

headline: New Delhi: Reacting to allegations by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi in Parliament Wednesday, Union Minister Jitendra Singh clarified that Home Minister Amit Shah could not have ordered the use of force or firing on students protesting against the...
full_text:
New Delhi: Reacting to allegations by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi in Parliament Wednesday, Union Minister Jitendra Singh clarified that Home Minister Amit Shah could not have ordered the use of force or firing on students protesting against the NEET question paper leak.
Singh said that no shots were fired, only tear gas was used at the Jantar Mantar protesters. He further said that Rahul Gandhi should be aware that orders are not issued by ministers but by magistrates, SDMs, or DMs.
“It was repeatedly clarified that no shots were fired; tear gas was used. Since no shots were fired, the question of issuing an order does not arise. The authority to issue such an order anyway rests with the magistrate, not the minister,” Singh said responding to opposition leader in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi who he said had claimed that Union Home Minister Amit Shah had given directions to open fire.
“Ye baar baar spasth kiya gaya ki goli chali hee nahi. Aansu gas (ka istemaal hua). Lekin jab goli chali hee nahi toh aadesh dene ka sawaal hee nahi paida hota. Aur aadesh dene ka adhikar magistrate ke paas rehta hai mantri ke paas nahi,” he said.
The minister further said that “utmost restraint was exercised” on 20 July during the Jantar Mantar protest.
“When such an important bill is being discussed, instead of offering suggestions, politics is being played over it. The unparliamentary language used by the Leader of the Opposition is shocking; it makes me wonder if he is even aware of basic parliamentary norms… What could be more unfortunate than calling the youth of this country—who are its future—’idiots’?” Singh said. The word was later expunged.
“If someone calls himself an idiot here, that’s also not allowed. The Leader of the Opposition does not know the basic norms of the House,” said Singh as he hit back at Gandhi’s remarks.
The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, aimed at implementing stricter provisions to prevent future paper leaks, was passed in the Lok Sabha Wednesday amid an Opposition walkout and furore over Rahul Gandhi’s remarks on Shah.
“Instead of engaging in a meaningful debate and offering constructive suggestions, the Opposition is trying to politicise the issue. I am particularly surprised by the conduct of the Leader of the Opposition. The words he used were not only unparliamentary but so inappropriate that I would not even repeat them here. If someone considers themselves educated and aware of parliamentary conventions, they would know that such language cannot be used inside the House. They may choose to say such things outside Parliament, but not within it. I am astonished that the Leader of the Opposition, who holds such an important constitutional position, appears to lack even a basic understanding of parliamentary norms and decorum,” he added.
Triggering sharp protests from BJP ministers Rajnath Singh and Kiren Rijiju, Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi had targeted Amit Shah, questioning the Union home minister’s absence from the House during the debate.
“The Home Minister is not here today because he is scared. He authorised the shooting of the students,” Rahul Gandhi alleged.
Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said that Gandhi should produce evidence of the charges he levelled against the Union home minister Amit Shah.
Rahul Gandhi also used what he said was an 18-year-old student’s description to attack the government, describing three kinds of people—students, (expunged word) and andhbhakts (blind followers).
Recounting a conversation, Rahul Gandhi said he had met the student during the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ protests. Quoting Mahatma Gandhi, Rahul said the windows of a student’s house are always open because they are willing to listen and learn.
“Truth is sweet. A student keeps running after the truth. Like Mahatma Gandhi said, the windows of a student’s house are open to all winds. The hallmark of a student is that the student wears the truth on his own chest, proudly. The other type requires an image because the (expunged word) is trying to pretend that he is God. These (expunged word) don’t listen to what anyone says,” Gandhi said.
The remarks immediately drew objections from the BJP. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju accused Rahul Gandhi of using a student’s words to make “unparliamentary” insinuations against political opponents and urged the Chair to intervene. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh also objected to the remarks and requested that the “unparliamentary” expressions be expunged from the record. Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav backed Rahul Gandhi’s statement during the heated exchanges.
The Congress leader then trained his guns on the Centre’s education policy. “Our education system is terrible, it is cruel. There is rampant privatisation. The soul of the education system has been captured by the RSS,” Gandhi alleged.
“Students are really irritated about not being allowed to follow their passion, to ask questions they want to,” he said.
Rahul Gandhi further alleged that universities across India had RSS-backed leadership and claimed that the RSS, and not Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan exercised real control over the education system. He also claimed that every university in the country had an RSS-linked chancellor and argued that the ideological capture of educational institutions had undermined independent thinking.
Praising the recent student protests over the paper leaks, Rahul Gandhi said the demonstrations reflected hope rather than anger. “I was very excited and reassured by what the future of this country did on our streets. This was not anger, violence or hatred, but a deep expression of the youth of this country, of the future generation of this country,” he said.
Urging all political parties to respect students, Rahul Gandhi said BJP leaders should ask their own children what they thought about the protests. “If BJP leaders ask their children, they will know they agree with the students on the streets,” he remarked.
The house was adjourned after Rahul’s speech.

headline: New Delhi: As the dust settles over the youth protest that took over the country over the past few weeks, a few prominent—and seemingly discordant—voices from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) have emerged.
full_text:
New Delhi: As the dust settles over the youth protest that took over the country over the past few weeks, a few prominent—and seemingly discordant—voices from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) have emerged.
Experts viewed the statements from various leaders as both critiquing and advising the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to course-correct.
From RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat to veteran BJP leaders and swayamsevaks Murli Manohar Joshi and Muralidhar Rao, as well as Sangh ideologue Ratan Sharda, senior Sangh leaders seemed uncomfortable with the way the government dealt with young protesters.
Last week, without referring to the young protesters, Mohan Bhagwat spoke about how the new generation asks questions and demands logic. He urged people to engage in dialogue with them instead of giving them orders.
Speaking at the valedictory session of a two-day national meeting on ‘Contemporary Motherhood’, Bhagwat called for a change in approach and style of engaging with the younger generation.
Ratan Sharda, who has written many books on the RSS, also came down heavily on the BJP’s media team, including its IT cell, in a post on social media platform X. He pointed to what he called a “total inability to create a narrative to counter hateful well crafted narrative of Left Ecosystem”.
However, he clarified that it was his “personal note” and had “nothing to do with RSS”.
Murli Manohar Joshi extended his support to the protest last week, criticising the use of “force” during the ‘Sansad Chalo’ protest march. In a post on X, Joshi wrote that such use of force “shall alienate large sections of Indian society from the national goal of Viksit Bharat”.
Joshi was the HRD minister in the Atal Bihari Vajpayee government and faced flak from political rivals for pushing the Sangh’s cultural agenda as the minister. Since 2014, Joshi has been in the political wilderness with no role in the party or the government.
Former BJP general secretary and ex-pracharak Muralidhar Rao also posted a veiled message on X, saying, “Governance may emerge from the mandate of the majority, but it endures only through the consent of the governed.”
Meanwhile, when Hindutva ideologue T.G. Mohandas made statements against the protests, threatening that he “would have shot” the protesters if he were in control, the RSS was quick to condemn the comments and distance itself from them.
Senior RSS functionary K.B. Sreekumar clarified that Mohandas is not an office-bearer of the RSS and called his remarks his “personal thoughts”. He said that the RSS does not agree with Mohandas’ comments and that “such views should be condemned in every highest possible manner”.
Political analysts see these remarks in the backdrop of massive protests across India, especially in New Delhi, led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak as part critiques, part advice and nudges for the BJP government to course correct.
Milan Vaishnav, senior fellow and director of the South Asia program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, says that there are concerns, including from within the Sangh, that the government has grown too distant from the common person, especially young people.
“I see these statements as nudges that aim to push the ruling party to be more engaged, more open to dialogue, and less insular. These tendencies to live inside a bubble tend to become more, not less, entrenched as time goes by,” he told ThePrint.
Ashutosh Varshney, political science professor at Brown University, also says that as a mother organisation, the RSS seems to be giving advice to the BJP.
The statements, he asserts, are “definitely a critique, not just a veiled critique; it’s a critique of the way the government has handled the youth. When it critiques the BJP, the RSS never says the BJP has betrayed the ideological mantle or ideological cause… It’s always a veiled argument, and the veiled argument is a hint and a suggestion. It’s part critique and part suggestion.”
Former editorial director at Swarajya magazine, senior journalist R. Jagannathan said that the statements point to a difference of opinion, and a message that the BJP could have handled the protests better.
Cautioning against viewing the BJP and the RSS with the same lens, he told ThePrint, “Though they definitely coordinate very closely with each other on some issues, they are not on the same page on all issues.”
“The statements by Bhagwat, Sharda, Rao and Joshi suggest that there is a difference between the RSS view of how things should be handled and how the BJP thinks it should handle them. Of course, the RSS is in an advisory capacity; it can say anything. The BJP has to govern, so it has to take its own call,” he says.
“I think it is an indirect advice to the government that everything cannot be done only through the legislature and executive action. You have to keep talking to people, and the mere act of talking actually can sort out some of the differences, even if you don’t necessarily agree,” he adds.
Owing to the month-long agitation, he says that “it is the right time for the RSS to tell the BJP that they look inwards for some of these mistakes”.
Also Read: Priyank Kharge escalates offensive against RSS, threatens legal action over its lack of registration
‘Daunting irreverence of the young’
A prominent critique of the youth protests has been the language used by some of the protesters. While humour and memes are part of their arsenal, the protest also saw abuses and insults hurled towards the government and its policies.
Varshney talks about this “daunting irreverence of the young”, saying, “It’s the extent to which Mr Modi was abused in very foul language by women, in particular young women, and so my expectation would have been that the RSS, in some form, would call it ‘Bharatiya sanskriti ke virudha’ (against Indian culture)… but this has not even been mentioned.”
Varshney then refers to Bhagwat’s statement, calling it the “most important of the lot”.
“His argument is that the older generation, when they were young, obeyed their parents and their elders. And this generation does not. He’s saying we have to accept that, and have a dialogue with them… It’s a very interesting formulation,” he says.
According to Varshney, the statement is a call to revive the “prachar and pracharak”, which is central to the RSS ideology of work.
“The idea is that through prachar and through pracharaks, you change young minds… The institution of Pracharak is the organisational core of the RSS strategy of work because the aim is to change the minds of the young more than anything else, so that the Hindu Rashtra that they have to establish would cease to be a dream and would become a reality one day,” he says.
“So, if the young minds are so angry that they can use language of the kind and the imagery of the kind that we saw on social media, then it’s the fault of prachar and pracharaks,” he adds.
The RSS, according to him, is therefore calling for different ways to do prachar and interact with the youth, “because the aim must remain changing the minds of the young”.
Specifically on Sharda’s tweet, Jagannathan says that it is the “sharpest comment” of the lot.
In his post, Sharda alleged that the BJP media seemed to have “no connect with the ground, no feedback mechanism obviously, and did not understand youth anger built over months, not just on NEET”.
NEET, he said, “was the straw on their back”. He wrote about the “total inability to create a narrative to counter hateful, well-crafted narrative of Left Ecosystem”, and said that the media team “didn’t go beyond memes or whataboutry”.
Sharda also defended his post, saying, “People like me speak from field experience, not Excel sheets or PPTs. My criticism 2024 served BJP wonderfully well. Yes, I will keep struggling for success of nationalist forces, support BJP but speak up where required (sic).”
Jagannathan says that Sharda’s comment was “more significant and more direct”.
“Communication means you must focus on your target audience. So I think what he (Sharda) is trying to say is that ‘Look, you (the BJP media team) are trying to please your bosses rather than trying to actually communicate with the audience that is supposed to listen to your advice and your messages’,” he explained.
‘Sane voices’
Instead of calling these discordant voices, a few experts call these statements “sane voices” of senior leaders.
Prof Chandrachur Singh, who teaches political science at Hindu College, says the problem is that the disillusionment of younger students is primarily because of the gap between the vision articulated by the government and the ways in which that vision has been rolled out.
He adds that the grievance of the younger generation is genuine, but also credits the government with having taken real steps, through the National Education Policy (NEP), to address structural issues in education. The gap, he says, is more about implementation and communication with intent.
“If you recall, Modi ji started his campaign in 2014 at SRCC. Somewhere I think that connect needs to be renewed and perhaps the government felt that having an NEP in place was enough of a signal. I think the government should build on that momentum and look not just into exam reform, but also at how educational institutions are governed,” he says.
In this context, Singh says that the statements by different leaders present a “saner voice” — one that strengthens the government’s own long-term goals rather than working against them.
“Coming from seniors like Mohan Bhagwat, or Murli Manohar Joshi, it’s really cautionary advice offered in good faith, which I think the BJP and the government will find useful to heed. It may sound discordant because there’s a perception that the RSS functions as a pressure group, but I don’t see it that way,” he says.
“It’s the voice of a well-wisher, someone invested in the government’s success.”
Rahul Verma, a fellow at Delhi-based think tank Centre for Policy Research, also says that he wouldn’t characterise these as discordant voices within the BJP.
“You can take comments from Murli Manohar Joshi or Mohan Bhagwat’s comments much more as advice from the elders of the party, who may be thinking that this is a difficult moment for the party and the government and how they should deal with it.”
“None of these voices in any way are attacking the government to call it open rebellion or completely discordant,” he told ThePrint.
Verma says that those who were protesting over the past month were mainly the younger generation, middle-class youth and their parents – which is a natural constituency of the BJP.
“If you see discontent or dissatisfaction among your own constituency, then it’s natural that there are going to be certain voices that are going to speak up,” he says.
Verma says the protest came at a time when the BJP government was also facing headwinds on other fronts, including economic anxiety and allegations of theft in the Ram Temple complex.
“So some people are going to point out that all is not well, and we need to be careful. And so, some sort of sane advice,” he adds.
‘Murmurs under the calm’
Some experts say the statements lay bare the internal voices of different factions within the party.
Senior journalist and political analyst Rasheed Kidwai asserts that although political parties often experience some level of disquiet and dissent, those voices may not be prominent in the case of a party in power and when there is a personality cult.
“But in a crisis situation, you do hear from all these voices… Not necessarily that these people are sidelined, but they have a view and they have a conscience, courage of conviction, and an ability to call a spade a spade. Politically and from a democratic point of view, it’s very welcoming because it keeps the leadership under some kind of check,” he says.
Kidwai also points to the larger issue of succession and different camps within the party.
“Nobody talks about it… There are many claimants, and in that sense, there are various camps (within the party), with people looking at their own future… And the role of RSS people is very important,” he says.
“Traditionally, the BJP cadre was very disciplined, but now, purely in terms of the legislative wing of the BJP, maybe 20 percent of people are outsiders… So on the surface it all looks calm and quiet, but below it, there are murmurs, and that is why you hear these voices.”
Verma also pointed to the possibility of such internal factionalism.
“All parties are made up of factions. There are always going to be competing interests in any party. So whenever the main leading faction of the party seems weaker, you would see other voices coming up,” says Verma.
“This is not to say that those who have made such statements recently belong to different factions of the BJP —they might or they might not—but these are all representative of different pressure groups within the party,” he adds.
“I still think that those voices have not come to attack or tarnish the image of the government. They have come more as raising concerns.”
Kidwai refers to the relationship between the RSS and the BJP as a philosopher-king relationship.
“When the philosopher is not heard, or the philosopher’s sagacious advice is not heeded, then the philosopher starts speaking differently, just to signal it to the king—hear me out,” he explains.
(Edited by Sugita Katyal)

headline: "In democracy, dialogue should always happen," said Chhagan Bhujbal.
full_text:
"In democracy, dialogue should always happen," said Chhagan Bhujbal.
NEW DELHI: Speculation over a possible reunion of the Nationalist Congress Party's two factions resurfaced on Thursday after senior leader Chhagan Bhujbal made fresh remarks on the issue, days after Sharad Pawar dismissed reports of a merger.Speaking to reporters during a visit to Pune, the Maharashtra minister was asked whether the rival NCP factions could come together. Responding to the question, Bhujbal said the decision rested with party president Sunetra Pawar and suggested there was little point in debating the matter until the leadership took a call.
"Deputy CM Sunetra Pawar is the (NCP) president, and a decision will be taken under her guidance. It is the media that fuels such speculation, so there is no point in discussing it. It will happen when it has to happen. Political leaders do meet one another on various issues. In democracy, dialogue should always happen."His comments came two days after NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar) chief Sharad Pawar rejected speculation over a possible merger of the two factions. Asked about the buzz by reporters on Tuesday, Pawar replied, "It has no relevance."
Bhujbal was in Pune to review the ongoing work at Bhidewada, the site where social reformers Mahatma Jyotirao Phule and Savitribai Phule started India's first school for girls.
After meeting officials of the Pune Municipal Corporation, the minister said the government wanted to preserve the legacy of Phule Wada and make its history accessible to students.
"...We want to showcase the history of Phule Wada to students. Rs 200 crore have been allocated for the expansion of Phule Wada. The chief minister has held meetings on the issue, but the work has not been completed in a satisfactory manner. We are ready to provide the land and we have completed all the necessary work," he said.Phule Wada, the former residence of Mahatma Jyotirao Phule and Savitribai Phule, is now a protected state heritage site and museum that commemorates their pioneering work in women's education and the fight against caste discrimination.

headline: New Delhi: Rajya Sabha member Surendra Singh Nagar Thursday made a pitch to the Centre to develop a single digital metro card valid across the entire country. Speaking during Zero Hour, the Bharatiya Janata Party MP said the existing practice of sepa...
full_text:
New Delhi: Rajya Sabha member Surendra Singh Nagar Thursday made a pitch to the Centre to develop a single digital metro card valid across the entire country. Speaking during Zero Hour, the Bharatiya Janata Party MP said the existing practice of separate plastic smart cards for every city creates unnecessary hardship for commuters and adds to environmental damage.
Placing the issue in the context of India’s expanding metro network, Nagar said that India ranks third in the world in terms of metro track length, with nearly 1,090 km already operational in about 24 cities and a comparable length under construction. He also mentioned the 2026-27 budget allocation of ₹28,740 crore for metro projects, calling it the highest so far.
Despite this growth, Nagar observed that passengers still face a fragmented ticketing system. A card bought in Delhi cannot be used in Bengaluru, just as a Bengaluru card is useless in Bhopal. Every city requires its own card, a separate balance and a different set of rules, causing inconvenience and generating plastic waste.
To resolve this, Mr. Nagar suggested a “One Nation, One Digital Metro Card”. The card, he explained, should be digital and account-based, linked to a passenger’s mobile number rather than being just a plastic card, so that one balance works on every metro network.
He listed three grounds for the proposal. On the environmental side, he noted that a metro smart card contains about five grams of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) along with a chip and antenna, making recycling extremely difficult. The material remains in the environment for as long as 500 years. Nearly six billion such cards are manufactured globally each year, and each contributes around 150 grams of carbon emissions. With digital options already available, Nagar questioned the wisdom of continuing large-scale plastic card distribution.
Turning to passenger rights, Nagar said that money stored in a physical card is often lost forever if the card is misplaced, damaged or expires. Many systems offer neither a blocking facility nor a refund, he said, adding that bank cards and Unified Payments Interface (UPI) accounts, in contrast, protect a user’s funds. A digital account-based system would keep the balance with the person; even if a mobile phone is unavailable, a passenger could still collect a Quick-Response (QR) ticket at a counter using a registered number, Nagar elaborated.
The MP ended his submission with three clear requests to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs: creation of a national interoperable digital metro card; gradual shift of all metro systems to QR and account-based ticketing; and a guarantee that balances remain fully secure, transferable and recoverable. He noted India’s leadership in digital payments through UPI and urged that the same spirit now be applied to public transport, so that travel becomes less dependent on plastic, less expensive to operate, more convenient and safer for every citizen.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

headline: 21-year-old dies after ambulance oxygen runs out in MP; probe ordered
full_text:
21-year-old dies after ambulance oxygen runs out in MP; probe ordered
Ajit Baraiya, a resident of Sunhara Mal village, died on July 27 while being transferred from Bamhani Hospital to Mandla with oxygen support
A 21-year-old died in Madhya Pradesh’s Mandla district allegedly after the oxygen supply in an ambulance cylinder ran out while he was being shifted to a district hospital, his father alleged.
Ajit Baraiya, a resident of Sunhara Mal village, died on July 27 while being transferred from Bamhani Hospital to Mandla with oxygen support. The administration has ordered an inquiry into the incident.
Mandla collector Rahul Namdev Dhote has constituted a four-member committee to probe the matter. “The committee has been instructed to submit its report at the earliest, based on which further action will be taken,” Dhote said.
Ajit’s father alleged that the cylinder ran out during the three-hour journey, leading to respiratory failure. The family also recorded a video showing the ambulance’s oxygen gauge at zero.
Collector Dhote said Ajit had been suffering from a severe kidney ailment for a long time. “He was referred to the district hospital with oxygen support. His father alleged that the cylinder ran out during the journey, causing his death,” Dhote said.
The opposition has raised the issue, demanding a high-level inquiry into the functioning of ambulance services in Madhya Pradesh. “There is a need to examine the working and facilities of the 108 services. This is a very serious matter, as a youth lost his life due to the negligence of ambulance attendants,” Congress MLA and former minister Jaivardhan Singh said.

headline: Delhi riots: Tahir Hussain, 4 others get life terms in IB staffer's murder case
full_text:
Delhi riots: Tahir Hussain, 4 others get life terms in IB staffer's murder case
While the court observed that the murder was ‘rarest of the rare’ case in terms of brutality, it rejected the Delhi Police’s plea for capital punishment.
Former Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) councillor Tahir Hussain and four others were on Friday sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of Intelligence Bureau (IB) officer Ankit Sharma during the 2020 Delhi riots, with a city court ruling that while the crime was “horrendous” and “sickening”, the prosecution had failed to prove that the convicts were beyond the possibility of reform.
Additional sessions judge Parveen Singh of the Karkardooma courts sentenced Hussain, and four others – Kasim, Nazim, Javed and Anas – to imprisonment for life.
Also read: 'Murderous mob dragged him': What happened the day IB official was killed in Delhi riots
The court rejected the Delhi Police’s plea for capital punishment. The court observed that although the murder fell within the “rarest of the rare” category on account of its brutality, the prosecution had not established that the convicts’ continued existence in prison “would pose a menace to society”.
Emphasising the severity of the crime, the court held: “The crime was brutal, with a murderous mob baying for blood of the victim… the manner and the utmost brutality with which the victim was killed was done solely on account of religion. He was sucked in by a murderous mob and strapped like an animal… and as if the hatred had still not been satiated, the dead body was thereafter thrown into the nala.”
Describing the killing as being committed in “utter disdain of law” and with complete “disregard for life”, the judge said the barbarity of the murder constituted an aggravating circumstance of the highest order.
Also read: 'Not too late, HC will ensure justice': Tahir Hussain on life term in Ankit Sharma murder case
The court rejected the convicts’ plea that their dependent families should be treated as a mitigating circumstance, holding that the “monstrosity of the crime outweighs that defence”.
To be sure, it held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the convicts were incapable of reformation. The judge noted that none of them had a history indicating a violent disposition or criminal propensity and that, barring minor prison infractions, their conduct in custody had been satisfactory. “This indicates that they can be disciplined and made to follow rule-based order,” the court observed.
ASJ Singh also declined to accept the prosecution’s frontal argument that Hussain had planned and facilitated the violence by allowing his house to be used for stockpiling petrol bombs and weapons.
Also read: 'Insaaf nahi hua hai': Tahir Hussain broke down after conviction in IB staffer's murder case
“No role has been attributed to Tahir Hussain and the allegation that he facilitated and instigated the mob and used his house as a base for petrol bombs has to be rejected as no evidence has been brought on record,” the judge said. “I find myself unable to believe that their continued existence even in prison would be a menace to society,” the court held.
In case of the four other convicts, the court treated their lack of education as a mitigating factor. While observing that illiteracy should not ordinarily reduce punishment, the judge held that they had become “susceptible to misinformation” and “communal frenzy” during the riots.
“The offence was committed when vested interests... whipped up a religious crime. The convicts, being uneducated, were more gullible and susceptible to such propaganda,” the court said, adding that persons with little or no education are generally less equipped to critically evaluate misinformation.
Last week, Delhi Police had sought the death penalty, describing the killing as “exceptionally brutal”, “cold-blooded” and among the “rarest of the rare” category. “Ankit Sharma was assaulted in a hapless manner… It is not a case where somebody was stabbed once or thrice,” special public prosecutor Madhukar Pandey argued.
A Delhi court on July 13 convicted Hussain and four others for Sharma’s murder, holding that Hussain, along with an “armed” mob, had carried out a “savage” and “relentless” attack.
Hussain, represented by advocate Rajiv Mohan, opposed the plea, arguing that there was no evidence of a criminal conspiracy or direct attribution of fatal injuries to him.
The five were convicted on July 13 for Sharma’s murder, while six others were acquitted.

headline: Delhi riots 2020: Why Tahir Hussain escaped death penalty in IB officer Ankit Sharma murder case
full_text:
Delhi riots 2020: Why Tahir Hussain escaped death penalty in IB officer Ankit Sharma murder case
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Jul 31, 2026, 17:12 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
