headline: Why Dharmendra Pradhan's homecoming has set the cat among pigeons in Odisha
full_text:
Why Dharmendra Pradhan's homecoming has set the cat among pigeons in Odisha
Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation as a Union minister and a hero's welcome in Bhubaneswar have reignited speculation over his next political move. Will one of the most formidable leaders of the BJP become the CM? Experts suggest that the road ahead depends on several factors.
A resignation in New Delhi has resulted in the politics in Odisha hotting up. While it was watching the fast-paced developments in neighbouring West Bengal, the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as Union Education Minister and him receiving a hero's welcome have sparked speculation over the BJP heavyweight's next political move.
For the uninitiated, Dharmendra Pradhan, who's the Lok Sabha MP from Sambalpur, is credited for building the party's organisational muscles in Odisha. He commands the loyalty of a large number of MLAs and ministers, and is an alternative power centre in the state.
While the BJP projected Pradhan's Odisha homecoming as a show of strength, political observers in Bhubaneswar see it as the start of speculation about the leader's next role in the state where he built the saffron party from scratch. The reception at Bhubaneswar airport, attended by several Odisha ministers and MLAs, made many ask if the BJP was planning to assign the top job in the state to him. Just the buzz that Pradhan could be positioned for the CM's role has unnerved some in Odisha's political circles, say experts.
The circumstances of Pradhan's resignation in New Delhi and the political mood in Odisha, however, make these speculations far from straightforward. Two Odisha-based political observers and an insider in the BJP's political circle in Odisha say, while Pradhan remains one of the BJP's most formidable leaders in the state, the road ahead would be based on calculations of the party high-command. However, they see him as a rightful claimant to the CM's post.
Dharmendra Pradhan resigned as Union Education Minister after the CJP-led agitation over alleged examination irregularities demanded he quit from the post on the grounds of accountability. Pradhan's return to the east-coastal state has ignited speculation over whether the saffron party is scripting a role change for the leader who's been part of the Narendra Modi Cabinet since 2014. Though Pradhan has resigned as a Union minister, he continues to be the Sambalpur MP.
A Bhubaneswar-based journalist, who spoke to India Today Digital on condition of anonymity, says speculation about Pradhan's return to state politics has unsettled internal equations and "set the cat among the pigeons". We'll get into the explanation of why the journalist said so. But before that, let's first have a look at how Pradhan's resignation has gone down with people in Odisha.
A HERO'S WELCOME, BUT ALSO AN IMAGE RESET FOR PRADHAN?
Bhubaneswar-based senior journalist and political commentator Rajaram Satpathy says the optics of Pradhan's welcome at the Bhubaneswar airport were significant and noteworthy.
"Having relinquished his post as Union education minister in the face of fierce agitation over the NEET-UG question paper leak, Dharmendra Pradhan came home Tuesday [July 28] for the first time as an MP. There was, however, a good crowd at the airport to welcome him. The scene was reminiscent of the welcome NDA MPs gave him outside Parliament recently. Five of 16 ministers of the Mohan Charan Majhi-led government and 21 party MLAs were on hand to receive him," Satpathy tells India Today Digital.
Satpathy also says that he believes the reception carried a political message. "Observers view the heroic welcome accorded to Pradhan as a desperate image make-over bid to sustain him in politics in the days ahead," explains Satpathy.
Despite the setback, Satpathy argues that Pradhan's stature within the BJP remains significant.
"Close to the BJP top brass in New Delhi, Pradhan is rated an influential national Odia leader after [former Odisha chief ministers] Biju Patnaik and Harekrushna Mahatab. He is also credited with building the BJP's state unit almost from scratch to what it is today," says Satpathy.
However, he says Pradhan's resignation has altered some public perceptions in Odisha.
"Sadly, his public image belies his political standing. It certainly took a beating after the students' agitation that forced him to finally put in his papers after all efforts reportedly to retain him in the ministry failed," says Satpathy, adding that the public opinion on Pradhan in Odisha remains divided.
"People in Odisha, though, feel sad that an influential Odia in the Union government was sacrificed. However, they are divided," Satpathy tells India Today Digital. "His critics justify his resignation, saying he failed to foresee the approaching danger despite being so experienced in government functioning. Pradhan, they say, could have done more to check the recurring chaos in one exam after another."
The big question is where Dharmendra Pradhan goes from here. Interestingly, Pradhan was considered a frontrunner for the chief minister's post after the BJP won the Assembly elections in Odisha for the first time in 2024. However, the BJP high command chose Mohan Charan Manjhi, a four-time MLA from the tribal community representing the Keonjhar seat, to be the CM.
The move was seen by some as a signal from the BJP ahead of the Jharkhand Assembly polls, which the party lost.
WHAT NEXT FOR DHARMENDRA PRADHAN?
For now, Satpathy says there is little certainty about Pradhan's immediate future. But he points to two possibilities.
"There is speculation on two things. He may lie low for some time, or the BJP may give him some party post and use him in organisational work," Satpathy tells India Today Digital.
However, discussion around Pradhan's future inevitably circles back to Odisha's top post, given his journey from an ABVP leader to one of the principal architects of the BJP's organisation in a state long dominated by the Biju Janata Dal (BJD) led by former CM Naveen Patnaik.
Satpathy recalls that after the BJP's historic victory in 2024, Pradhan was seen as a contender. Asked whether that possibility could revive now, Satpathy remains unconvinced. "No. Distant possibility," he says.
He also dismisses comparisons between "a timid" Mohan Charan Majhi and the BJP's selection of firebrand leader Suvendu Adhikari in neighbouring West Bengal as the party's face.
"Whether Pradhan stands a chance to be the CM in view of the contrast in dynamism between the Odisha CM and his West Bengal counterpart is all speculation," Satpathy tells India Today Digital.
WHAT WORKS IN DHARMENDRA PRADHAN'S FAVOUR IN ODISHA?
Even though he has been in New Delhi for a considerable period of time (first as an MP since 2004 and then as a Union minister since 2014), Satpathy believes "Pradhan commands the support of a sizeable number of people in the party," Satpathy says, pointing to the airport reception in the state capital as evidence.
"Pradhan is a big force in Odisha politics, and he claims the loyalty of at least 40 BJP MLAs, especially the younger ones," says a Bhubaneswar-based journalist, who requested anonymity. He tells India Today Digital that Pradhan's organisational influence in Odisha remains formidable.
The BJP has 79 MLAs in the 147-member Odisha Assembly.
An insider from within the Odisha BJP spoke about a dinner that was attended by ministers and MLAs. "There was discussion on the Assembly seats that could be vacated for Pradhan to contest from," the person said.
The source said that there was a high possibility that the seat could be from Jharsuguda, which neighbours Sambalpur and is part of the Bargarh Lok Sabha constituency.
The journalist who didn't want to be named, however, believes that the BJP leadership, which might want Pradhan at the helm in Odisha in the long run, is unlikely to make any immediate leadership changes.
"The Delhi stint certainly has made Dharmendra Pradhan more experienced, but not an edge in Odisha politics, given the wind currently blowing against him," political commentator Satpathy tells India Today Digital.
ALL WELL WITHIN BJP IN ODISHA? IS RESURGENT BJD CATCHING UP?
Firstly, despite the goodwill of Odisha's first tribal Chief Minister, dissatisfaction over governance and crime has surfaced within political circles. CM Majhi's delivery is under scrutiny. The recent local body election in CM's Keonjhar did not go that well for the BJP. According to a report in The New Indian Express newspaper, out of the 21 wards of Keonjhar municipality, the BJD won 13 seats while the remaining eight went to the BJP.
CM Mohan Charan Majhi is the MLA from Keonjhar.
"There is a resurgence in pro-BJD sentiments for the first time since the BJP swept the polls in 2024... The BJP's setback in the Keonjhar municipality and the boost to the BJD following Sujata Rout Karthikeyan's entry into the party might prevent the BJP brass from promoting Pradhan immediately," the Bhubaneswar-based journalist says.
Sujata Rout Karthikeyan, a former IAS officer and wife of VK Pandian — the bureaucrat-turned-aide of BJD chief Naveen Patnaik — joined the party in June, almost two years after the regional party suffered a rout from the state it ruled for 24 years uninterrupted.
The party, needful of a robust second-rung leadership, found a helping hand in Sujata Rout's husband, VK Pandian. A person of Tamil origin, he wielded considerable influence as the CM’s private secretary, played a central role in governance, and was even called Patnaik's heir-apparent by many.
Pandian, following the BJD's defeat in the 2024 elections, faced backlash. He stepped away from politics, taking moral responsibility. With Rout entering politics, the BJD is rebuilding itself. Pandian's wife, Rout, is from Kendrapara district. Patnaik called her Sujata Rout instead of Sujata Rout Karthikeyan, according to a report in The Hindu.
WHY BJP MAY NOT BE IN A HURRY TO AWARD PRADHAN ODISHA's TOP POST
The journalist from Odisha who spoke on the condition of anonymity says that he believes replacing the current CM could create fresh complications. "Asking Manjhi to step down could become a 'tribal issue' while crowning Pradhan, who was forced to resign as a Union minister, might not go down well among the younger population," he says.
He adds that even speculation about Pradhan returning to state politics has unsettled internal equations in the state unit of the BJP. "The buzz of Pradhan returning to state politics had set the cat among the pigeons."
"Aparajita Sarangi, Baijayant Jay Panda and Manmohan Samal wouldn't be too excited," he says, pointing to the BJP heavyweights in Odisha. Manjhi, he explains, started from the Dharmendra Pradhan camp but has lately aligned himself with Manmohan Samal.
Sarangi is a former IAS officer-turned-politician and serves as an MP representing the Bhubaneswar Lok Sabha seat. Baijayant Jay Panda is an industrialist-politician and is the National Vice-President for the BJP. Samal leads the BJP's Odisha Unit.
"The BJP brass, if it has decided to make Pradhan the Odisha CM, might choose to wait for five to six months before going ahead with the plan," the journalist tells India Today Digital, adding that perceptions about the former Union minister differ across generations in the state.
"A big chunk of the people over 40 in Odisha think that Pradhan will bring about change. He will be a better CM than Majhi. Even those who don't support the BJP think Pradhan will do a better job," he says. The journalist said making Pradhan the CM immediately might make the BJP "the target of youth, especially Gen Z, ire. That's because of the baggage he carries from Delhi," the Odisha-based journalist adds.
To conclude, time will tell whether Pradhan's future lies in Bhubaneswar and when that time comes. The Delhi exit has certainly opened an opportunity for a chapter in Odisha. People on the ground say Pradhan could be an organisational strategist for the party with a pan-India role or could enter state politics. The question is how long the cooling-off period would be. The recent chain of events has definitely ignited debates over leadership even as Pradhan continues to enjoy New Delhi's backing. Will the BJP's next political move in Odisha determine Pradhan's future? The picture might be clear in a few months.

headline: Residents of the Scheduled Tribe settlement at Thoppilayi near Kakkanpara in Sreekandapuram municipality, Kannur, suspended their 17-day protest against a laterite quarry on Sunday (August 2, 2026) after the District Collector issued a temporary stop...
full_text:
Residents of the Scheduled Tribe settlement at Thoppilayi near Kakkanpara in Sreekandapuram municipality, Kannur, suspended their 17-day protest against a laterite quarry on Sunday (August 2, 2026) after the District Collector issued a temporary stop memo halting quarrying.
Protest committee convenor P. Bindu, who had been on a fast for nine days, and Uru Mooppan P. Aneesh, who continued the fast for three days, ended their hunger strike.
The protest committee alleged that a private individual had purchased land originally allotted to landless families for house construction under a surplus land scheme and obtained permission for laterite mining using fabricated documents. Residents of the tribal settlement said quarrying on the ecologically sensitive laterite hill posed a serious threat to around 50 Scheduled Tribe families living nearby. They also expressed concern that their cremation ground, community building, and drinking water tank, located close to the quarry site, could be endangered.
The quarry owners had resumed mining under police protection after securing a favourable order from the High Court. In response, the protest committee launched a relay hunger strike 13 days ago, with five people participating in different phases.
District Collector P. Vishnuraj issued the temporary stop memo after inquiries by the Department of Mining and Geology and other departments, following petitions submitted by the protest committee to the Collector and other authorities challenging the quarry permit.
The inquiry reportedly found that a public road lies within a 50-metre radius of the quarry, prompting the temporary suspension of mining.
Residents said attempts to start the laterite quarry had been made since 2023 but were abandoned following public opposition. After obtaining a favourable High Court order, the owners resumed quarrying, triggering protests by residents of the tribal settlement.
Earlier, P. Chandran and M. Remeshan, who had undertaken the initial phase of the hunger strike, were hospitalised after their health deteriorated. They were succeeded by P. Bindu and E. Shyamala. Ms. Shyamala was also admitted to hospital three days ago after her condition worsened, following which P. Aneesh continued the fast.
The Taliparamba Revenue Divisional Officer and the Tahsildar had earlier held discussions with the protesters and assured them that action would be taken against the quarry. On Saturday (August 3, 2026) afternoon, the Tahsildar reached the protest venue and read out the District Collector’s stop memo, after which the protest committee decided to suspend the agitation.
The protest committee said a public meeting would be held at the protest venue at 11 a.m. on Monday (August 3, 2026) to decide the future course of the agitation.

headline: After PM's forgiveness, Delhi Police drops case against minor who abused him
full_text:
After PM's forgiveness, Delhi Police drops case against minor who abused him
Delhi Police have decided not to pursue a case against the 15-year-old girl seen abusing Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a viral protest video, citing her age, apology, and appeals for leniency. The decision also follows PM Modi's public statement that he had forgiven the "misguided children."
The Delhi Police will not go ahead with the FIR filed against the minor girl seen in a viral video using expletives against Prime Minister Narendra Modi during the Cockroach Janta Party's protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar last month.
The decision comes despite a Zero FIR being lodged by Noida Police. The accused later issued an apology video, claiming she is 15 years old and alleging that she made the remarks under the influence of others at the protest site.
In the video released earlier this week, the girl said, “I am only 15 years old. Whatever I did was not worthy of forgiveness. I have said a lot of bad things. This is my first and last mistake. I apologise to the entire country. I am so ashamed. I can't even look at myself. Please forgive me.”
As appeals for leniency gained traction on social media, PM Modi last Friday said that he had forgiven the “misguided children” who had abused him. In an Instagram reel, he said, “Punishing them and dragging them through courts and harassing them will not change the circumstances. I want to forgive them. I request society also to accept what I am saying.”
The girl's mother had also appealed to the Prime Minister to ask the authorities to withdraw the FIR. She said, “PM Modi has shown greatness by forgiving a daughter of the country who had used such dirty words. I thank him with folded hands. Today is her new birth. The prime minister has given her jeevandaan (a new life).”
“I request Prime Minister Narendra Modi, please revoke the FIR filed against her under the wrong name and age... Now she is under your supervision,” she said.
The mother also urged the Prime Minister to ban social media access for minors. “My humble request to PM Modi is that Instagram and Facebook should be stopped for children under 18. They should be allowed to study only. They should not be allowed to protest sites. These children can be easily taken advantage of. They don't know anything about the world,” she said. The case had drawn attention after the video went viral, but Delhi Police have now decided not to proceed against the minor.
STUDENTS PROTEST AT JANTAR MANTAR
The youth-led CJP protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi ended on July 25 after days of mobilisation over the large-scale leaking of papers for competitive examinations. Thousands of student activists took part in the protest, which drew support from innovator-activist Sonam Wangchuk, who joined the agitation during his 26-day hunger strike.
The demonstrations intensified over the course of the protest, with police standoffs and a major march to Parliament on July 20 becoming key developments in the agitation. The protest also led to the resignation of then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The CJP later announced the end of the protest after the government accepted its main demands, including education reforms to improve transparency and accountability in competitive examinations.
The agitation at Jantar Mantar was centred on public anger over the paper leaks in competitive examinations. Student activists gathered in large numbers to press for action, while Wangchuk's participation during his hunger strike added to the visibility of the protest. As the demonstrations grew, confrontations with the police and the march towards Parliament marked a major phase of the campaign.
With the government agreeing to the core demands raised by the protesters, the CJP formally concluded the agitation on July 25. The protest had focused on examination paper leaks, demands for reforms in the education system, and calls for stronger transparency and accountability in the conduct of competitive examinations.

headline: Eluru District Collector K. Vetri Selvi on Sunday appealed to citizens to share their feedback on services provided through the Public Grievance Redressal System (PGRS) by scanning QR codes displayed at district and mandal-level centres.

headline: Trekking policy gives livelihood push for tribals
full_text:
Trekking policy gives livelihood push for tribals
For generations, the Malekudiya people of Karnataka’s Western Ghats knew every bend in the forest-trails, every medicinal plant and every bird call
For generations, the Malekudiya people of Karnataka’s Western Ghats knew every bend in the forest-trails, every medicinal plant and every bird call. That knowledge rarely translated into economic security. Today, it has become their profession.
A new trekking policy introduced by Karnataka’s forest department has turned members of the indigenous forest dwelling community into certified nature guides, creating a steady source of income while placing those most familiar with the landscape at the centre of the visitor experience.
More than 60 members of the Malekudiya tribe have been certified to guide trekkers on the Nethravathi Peak trail alone. Others from the community now work on the Kudremukh, Gangadikal and Kurinjal trekking routes. Across Karkala, Belthangady, Sringeri and villages surrounding the Kudremukh forests, more than 350 local residents have found employment as certified trek guides.
Since April 2026, the forest department has required certified guides on all approved trekking routes. Every group of ten trekkers must be accompanied by one guide, daily visitor numbers on major trails are capped at 300, and bookings are made exclusively through the department’s online portal. The policy has opened employment opportunities for communities living inside the forests where the trekking routes are located.
For Manjunath Malekudiya, 50, of Malavanthige village in Belthangady taluk, the change has altered both how he earns a living and how visitors experience the forest.
Once he walked the Nethravathi Peak trail simply as part of daily life. Now he introduces trekkers to the Western Ghats through the names, stories and traditions he grew up with, identifying birds and plants using the Malekudiya language.
“I started as a guide three years ago. I had no formal training, but whenever I was called by local transport drivers who brought trekkers to the Nethravati Trek base camp, I would help out. Prior to this, I worked as a daily wage labourer and also on our agricultural land to earn my living. Over the years, as I started to age, I received less daily wage work. Working as a guide has now helped me earn a good income. On average, I earn about ₹15,000 to ₹20,000 per month when the trek season is on. During the other times, I work on my agricultural land. I haven’t gone guiding for the last two weeks as I am busy ploughing my land,” he said.
He is now among those formally trained and certified by the forest department.
Ashok Malekudiya, 24, from Elaneeru village, is among the few people in his community to complete a bachelor’s degree. Instead of leaving in search of work elsewhere, he chose to stay. “I never wanted to move out from here. Now, I have worked as a nature guide for three years and was certified a few months ago,” he said. “I earn about ₹15,000 to ₹20,000 per month.”
For younger members of the community, guiding has become an alternative to agricultural labour.
Nithin Malekudiya left school after SSLC and now works as a certified guide. Unlike his father, Uday Malekudiya, who depended on areca nut plantations and other farm labour, he sees tourism as a more secure livelihood.
“I work as a trek guide and get three to four assignments a week, which helps me earn a good amount. The days I am out of work, I help my father at home. This initiative has given us a new life; otherwise, we would have relied only on daily wage work or would have been forced to move out in search of better jobs,” he said.
His father said previous generations relied on physically demanding agricultural work or the collection of non-timber forest products such as wild honey, shikakai, Malabar tamarind, Ramapatra and medicinal herbs, an activity that is no longer permitted. He recalled earning only ₹250 for a full day’s labour and said many people who climbed areca nut trees had suffered life changing falls. “Compared to this, being a trek guide is a good option,” he said.
The community’s familiarity with the forest has become its greatest asset. Born and raised in the Western Ghats, the guides possess detailed knowledge of the terrain, wildlife and medicinal plants, which they now share with visitors during the treks.
V Sarmishta of the Belthangady Wildlife Range said the Nethravathi Peak jurisdiction currently has about 115 certified guides, including 60 from the Malekudiya community.
“Before becoming guides, these members of the tribal community had no proper income, working as daily wage labourers and doing other agricultural jobs. Some of them even used to travel to the Kalasa and Samse border areas of Dakshina Kannada and Chikkamagaluru for work. However, after becoming certified guides, they have had a stable income. As per our estimate, each person earns at least a minimum income of ₹12,000 per month. The trekkers also leave them tips, apart from a fixed daily salary of ₹1,000 per trek,” she said.
The Nethravathi Peak trail remains open from June until January or February, depending on the risk of forest fires. The route receives around 300 bookings each day, requiring roughly 30 to 35 guides daily under the one guide for every ten trekkers rule. Some visitors hire a guide even for groups of two or three.
Before receiving certification, all selected guides underwent training in personality development, visitor interaction and emergency response, including first aid and CPR, before being issued official certificates.
For a community, that had its understanding of the forest built over generations, the work has become more than seasonal employment. Knowledge once passed from parents to children is now helping sustain families while introducing visitors to the landscape through the people who have always called it home.

headline: Check my scholarship letter: Dipke counters RTI activist over US education row
full_text:
Check my scholarship letter: Dipke counters RTI activist over US education row
Abhijeet Dipke said a Boston University scholarship and an education loan funded his studies in the US after an RTI activist sought a probe into his family's finances. The exchange came as questions over the Cockroach Janta Party's funding, legal status and protest support sharpened.
Just a day after an RTI activist sought a probe into Abhijeet Dipke's family finances, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder asserted that a Boston University scholarship and an education loan paid for his studies in the US.
Speaking to senior journalist Barkha Dutt, Dipke rejected suggestions that his higher education abroad was funded through unexplained family wealth.
"My education was funded by a scholarship provided by Boston University. And I had taken some education loan which I have to pay back now," Dipke said, while also revealing his scholarship letter.
On August 1, Surat-based Amit Tiwari filed complaints with multiple authorities, including the Maharashtra government, seeking a probe into the finances of Dipke's father, Bhagwanrao Dipke, a retired Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation (MIDC) junior engineer.
Tiwari questioned how a government employee allegedly earning around Rs 60,000-65,000 a month could afford to send his children to the US for higher education.
During the interview, Dipke also addressed questions over how the CJP plans to finance its activities in the future.
"The CJP will do crowdfunding going forward where we will be asking money from people, and we will be very transparent about it," he said.
Recalling the nationwide anti-NEET paper leak agitation, Dipke claimed much of the support came directly from ordinary citizens.
"It should be very clear. The people who came to the protests saw that people were donating us food. The people brought their own water bottles," he said.
Dipke further claimed that some Delhi Police personnel had privately expressed support for the movement.
"Some people from the Delhi Police came to us and said, 'We will provide you with water bottles, but do not reveal our identities.' They said some of their children were also preparing for NEET, and they were sympathetic towards the cause, and that's why they wanted to give us water bottles," he alleged.
The CJP's finances have come under increased scrutiny after Kapil Sibal announced a Rs 1 crore legal aid fund for protesters arrested during the anti-NEET paper leak agitation.
The RTI activist has also approached the Election Commission of India over the legal status of the CJP and sought scrutiny of Sibal's aid.
Besides Dipke, CJP spokesperson Vaishnavi Gaur also hit back at the RTI activist, accusing him of selectively targeting a private individual.
"Those filing RTIs over a private individual's education expenses should also look at the PM CARES Fund. Modi ji will forgive you, don't worry," Gaur said in a post on X.
As questions over the outfit's funding and legal status intensified, the CJP dismissed the complaints as politically motivated.

headline: Rifle snatched, bullets fired, Jharkhand gangster killed in police encounter
full_text:
Rifle snatched, bullets fired, Jharkhand gangster killed in police encounter
Gangster Sujit Sinha was killed in a police encounter after an alleged escape bid during his transfer from Sahibganj Divisional Jail to Dhanbad Jail. Police have sealed the site and said standard legal procedures are under way.
One of Jharkhand's most wanted gangsters, Sujit Sinha, was killed in a police encounter late Sunday night after allegedly attempting to escape while being shifted from Sahibganj Divisional Jail to Dhanbad Jail.
According to police, the incident took place near the Jamtara border during the prison transfer. Officials said Sinha requested that the convoy stop so he could use the toilet. As the police vehicle halted, he allegedly snatched a rifle from one of the escort personnel and fled into the darkness.
Police claimed the gangster opened fire on the escort team while trying to escape, forcing officers to retaliate. During the exchange of fire, Sinha sustained serious bullet injuries.
He was immediately taken to a nearby hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
The encounter marked the end of the gangster who had long been on the radar of Jharkhand Police and was facing multiple criminal cases.
Following the incident, the encounter site was sealed as senior police officers rushed to the spot and reviewed the sequence of events.
Police said all aspects of the encounter are being examined and standard legal procedures are being followed.

headline: Chennai: Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi has drawn sharp criticism from the titular head of the Ettayapuram Samasthanam (a prominent historical feudal estate in Thoothukudi) after describing supporters of th...
full_text:
Chennai: Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi has drawn sharp criticism from the titular head of the Ettayapuram Samasthanam (a prominent historical feudal estate in Thoothukudi) after describing supporters of the proposed delimitation exercise as “21st-century Ettappans”, a term used in Tamil Nadu as a metaphor for traitor.
At an event in Mahabalipuram Saturday, Rahul Gandhi described the Centre’s proposed delimitation as a “BJP conspiracy” designed to disenfranchise the people of Tamil Nadu and strip the state of political power. He urged all Tamil parties and national parties to defeat the move in Parliament. He added, “Anyone who supports delimitation is betraying Tamil Nadu, betraying the future of Tamil Nadu, and allowing the RSS and BJP to attack the people of Tamil Nadu and its future. Such a person is a 21st-century Ettappan.”
Rahul Gandhi’s remarks come amid speculation that the Centre may revive a Constitutional amendment bill linked to increasing Lok Sabha seats and implementing women’s reservation, with concerns in southern states that the exercise could reduce their relative representation if based solely on population.
Rahul’s dig was aimed at DMK given that the party’s stance against delimitation is believed to have softened after they initially opposed the Delimitation Bill as the party has not presented a stern stance yet amid talks of the revival.
On Sunday, Chandra Chaitanya, the 42nd titular ‘Raja’ of the Ettayapuram Samasthanam hit back, urging Gandhi not to drag the family’s name into political battles. “Firstly, I really sincerely hope that you, Rahul Gandhi, will take a moment to learn about the actual history of Ettayapuram Samasthanam,” he said. He highlighted the family’s pioneering roles in girls’ education from the late 1800s, the first midday meal scheme in Tamil Nadu, and early participation in the temple entry movement.
“Despite all this, if somebody is still telling you that we were traitors to anyone… in fact, nobody bearing the name of Ettappan has ever betrayed anyone and if somebody is still feeding these lines to you, they are only feeding you the script of a movie, which has nothing to do with actual history,” Chaitanya told ANI. He stressed that public statements involving historical references must be factually accurate, noting that such usage undoes efforts to correct a false portrayal. “Do not use us as collateral damage in your political war of words,” he said.
In colloquial Tamil usage, ‘Ettappan’ is used as a derogatory term for a betrayer or traitor. The stigma around the word stems from the 1959 Tamil film ‘Veerapandiya Kattabomman’, starring Sivaji Ganesan, which depicted the ruler of Ettayapuram as having betrayed the chieftain Veerapandiya Kattabomman of Panchalankurichi to the British East India Company in the late 18th century. Kattabomman was captured and hanged by the British in 1799, and popular narratives and the film attributed a key role in his downfall to Ettappa Raja.
However, historical accounts also state that there were longstanding border disputes and raids between Ettayapuram and Panchalankurichi, with Ettayapuram aligning with the British against Kattabomman at certain points. However, Kattabomman was ultimately captured with assistance from the ruler of Pudukkottai, Vijaya Raghunatha Tondaiman, and handed over to the British.
Descendants of the Ettayapuram family and some historians maintain that the “betrayal” narrative is inaccurate or exaggerated, originating more from hearsay and cinema than actual history, and that no one bearing the name Ettappan betrayed Kattabomman in the manner portrayed in the film. The family argues that the modern pejorative represents a profound historical injustice that has even entered textbooks.
Raja Chandra Chaitanya has been campaigning to remove this “slur”, including approaching former Tamil Nadu Education Minister Anbil Mahesh for corrections in school textbooks and organising public demonstrations to educate people on the Samasthanam’s history of resistance and social reform rather than treachery. He has previously stated that the film’s depiction wounds the sentiments of Ettayapuram’s people and that the family will not accept a false burden indefinitely.
Political analyst Sunil Kumar explains that the word ‘Ettappan’ has been used in a derogatory manner for many years in Tamil Nadu because it is believed that he sided with the British.
Speaking about Rahul Gandhi, Kumar said, “He did not name DMK but his remarks seem to be directed at DMK. However, DMK has repeatedly said that they will not support delimitation if it is an infringement on the rights of Tamil Nadu people. DMK is not a part of INDIA alliance, so Rahul is making indirect moves to attack DMK and trigger their stance,” Sunil Kumar told ThePrint.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

headline: Gurugram: Former Haryana chief minister Bhupinder Singh Hooda has demanded that the state’s Commonwealth Games gold medallists be appointed Deputy Superintendents (DSP) in the Haryana Police. Reviving a decade-old political argument over how the stat...
full_text:
Gurugram: Former Haryana chief minister Bhupinder Singh Hooda has demanded that the state’s Commonwealth Games gold medallists be appointed Deputy Superintendents (DSP) in the Haryana Police. Reviving a decade-old political argument over how the state should reward its athletes, Hooda used social media platform X to invoke the ‘Padak Lao, Pad Pao (get a medal, get a post)’ scheme that his Congress government ran between 2005 and 2014.
Accusing the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of tampering with the system to deny athletes their due once it came to power, Hooda said the policy had built Haryana into a sporting powerhouse, and credited it with laurels the state’s players continue to bring home.
“This is not the first time our players have raised the flag high at the Commonwealth Games, they did the same in 2010. Our players are extremely talented and we’re proud of their hard work. It is the result of the ‘Padak Lao, Pad Pao’ policy we introduced that Haryana’s players continue to bring glory to the country,” Hooda told ThePrint.
He further said: “We built the sports infrastructure, set up academies, turned Haryana into a sports hub, and gave the youth the right direction; the results are visible even today. The boxing academy in Bhiwani was opened during our tenure, and today our daughters from there are lighting up the world stage.”
He added that the BJP government had undone what Congress built. “They have tampered with the policy we made and denied players their rewards, their honours, their positions. Even the players we appointed as DSPs haven’t been promoted under this government,” he said.
The demand lands on the back of a rich Glasgow haul. Six of Haryana’s boxers won gold at the Commonwealth Games — Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria and Sakshi Chaudhary, all from Bhiwani, in the women’s draw, and Priya Ghanghas, also of Bhiwani, alongside Sachin Siwach and Ankush Panghal among the men. Hisar’s Narender Berwal took silver in the +90kg category. Panipat’s Neeraj Chopra added a javelin silver, his second Commonwealth Games medal after the 2018 gold at Gold Coast.
Haryana Police records back up the part of Hooda’s claim about his government’s track record. Between 2005 and 2014, some 13 sportspersons were recruited as DSPs on the state Cabinet’s recommendation, using powers under Rule 14 of the Punjab Police Service Rules, 1959, to grant relaxations for exceptional appointments. The list includes hockey players Mamta Kharab, Sardar Singh and Surinder Kaur; wrestlers Geetika Jakhar, Ramesh Kumar, Ravinder Singh Sangwan and Yogeshwar Dutt; boxers Jitender Kumar, Akhil Kumar, Vijender Singh, Vikas Krishan and Paramjeet Samota; kabaddi player Mamta Sodha; and cricketer Joginder Sharma.
Sandeep Singh left the force to contest the 2019 Assembly election from Pehowa, won, and was made sports minister — before being booked on a molestation complaint by a woman athlete and dropped from the Cabinet when Nayab Singh Saini took over as chief minister.
Yogeshwar Dutt tried the same route from Baroda in 2019 and lost to Sri Kishan Hooda. In 2020, Dutt was fielded yet again by the BJP in a byelection to Baroda Assembly seat necessitated by Sri Kishan Hooda’s death, but he lost to Congress candidate Induraj Narwal. The BJP didn’t field Dutt in in the 2024 Assembly elections, but he continues to be a BJP leader.
Boxer Vijender Singh quit his DSP’s job when he turned professional in 2015. He joined the Congress ahead of 2019 election. However, he quit Congress and turned up unannounced at the BJP office to join the party ahead of the 2024 Assembly elections.
Also Read: Bhiwani’s boxer factory delivers 5 golds in Glasgow—a reminder of why it’s dubbed India’s ‘mini Cuba
Post-Hooda era
Since 2014, the Khattar as well as the Saini governments have moved away from discretionary appointments toward a rules-based framework, the Haryana Outstanding Sportspersons Service Rules, alongside cash award slabs for medal winners that have themselves been revised more than once.
Under the revised norms, sportspersons can compete for jobs in Group A, B and C under the Outstanding Sportsperson (OSP) cadre based on their achievements in the sports.
A retired India Police Service officer, explaining the legal architecture behind the old appointments to ThePrint, said the underlying law leaves little room for a standing scheme of the kind Congress ran. Regular DSP appointments go through the Haryana Public Service Commission or fixed promotion quotas, 80 per cent by promotion, and 20 per cent direct recruitment, under rules framed under Article 309 of the Constitution. The Cabinet’s Rule 14 power, he said, was meant for genuinely exceptional cases, such as the appointment of K.K. Rao on compassionate grounds after his father, DSP Ranbir Singh, was killed by terrorists in March 1989.
That power, he said, was used more loosely after 2005. He cited Mamta Sodha, an Everester appointed DSP though mountaineering has no recognised competitive sporting body, and Joginder Sharma, a Rohtak cricketer given the post despite never having played an Olympic sport.
The officer added that the record of sports-quota DSPs inside the force has been mixed, with most of those appointed showing weak outcomes on professionalism, integrity and contribution to developing sport within the department itself.
He said that the sportspersons are normally busy in their sporting career and are hardly able to complete their training after induction into the police force. Also, the kind of expenditure a sportsperson has to incur on oneself for training and diet, cannot be logically met from the salary of a government officer even if one is a DSP. “Looking at their expertise, the government should make use of their talent at jobs where they can train the future generation of sportspersons,” he added.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

headline: 'Verify, demarcate wetlands in SAC Atlas within 2 months': Supreme Court issues directives for states
full_text:
'Verify, demarcate wetlands in SAC Atlas within 2 months': Supreme Court issues directives for states
The court directed states and Union territories to physically verify and demarcate all wetlands identified in the SAC Atlas.
The Supreme Court has tightened its oversight of the protection of India’s wetlands, directing the Centre, states and Union territories to physically verify and demarcate all wetlands identified in the Space Applications Centre (SAC) Atlas within two months, while warning that secretaries and other senior officials will be summoned to court if the exercise remains confined to paperwork.
A bench of justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi made it clear that the statutory exercise of “ground-truthing” and boundary demarcation under the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, cannot be completed merely on paper and must involve physical identification of the wetlands on the ground.
“Ground truthing and demarcation of wetland boundary should not only be on paper but also to be physically carried out and identification of such wetlands or water bodies as identified by the SAC Atlas shall be undertaken by all the states if not already undertaken and a report be filed before this court expeditiously and at any rate within an outer limit of two months,” the bench directed in an order passed on July 28 and released on Saturday.
Also read: Conserving wetlands to nurture nature, society
Officials warned over non-compliance
The court added: “This exercise of physical verification if not undertaken, the Secretaries of Ministry of Environment and Forest and the Vice Chairman of the respective State Wetland Authorities shall appear in person on the next date of hearing and show cause as to why further steps should not be taken by this court for non-compliance,” adding that any breach of its present or previous directions would be viewed “very seriously”.
The latest order marks a significant escalation in litigation the top court has been monitoring since 2018 to ensure the identification, notification and protection of wetlands across the country. The proceedings arise from a batch of public interest litigations filed by Greater Noida-based birder and environmentalist Anand Arya, advocate MK Balakrishnan and NGO Vanashakti.
The court recalled that as far back as December 11, 2024, it had directed every state and UT Wetland Authority to complete “ground-truthing” and boundary demarcation of all wetlands identified in the 2021 SAC Atlas within three months, describing it as a statutory obligation under the Wetlands Rules. Those directions were reiterated in subsequent orders dated August 19, October 7 and October 28, 2025.
Also read: SC panel on Aravallis seeks stakeholder inputs for final report on definition of range
However, senior advocates Jayant Bhushan and Anitha Shenoy, appearing for the petitioners, informed the court that while several states claimed compliance, the exercise had largely remained a desk exercise. According to them, wetlands identified through satellite imagery had neither been physically inspected nor verified on site, defeating the very objective of ground-truthing before demarcation.
Accepting the submission, the bench observed that despite its repeated orders, some states and their wetland authorities were attempting to take a position contrary to the court’s directions.
“When our order dated 11.12.2024 which has been reiterated on 19.08.2025, 07.10.2025 and 28.10.2025 is clear, we fail to understand as to how the states or its instrumentalities or the Wetland Authorities...can take a different view,” the bench said before directing that both ground-truthing and demarcation should not only be on paper but also be physically carried out.
Two-month deadline for physical verification
The direction effectively gives all states and UTs a final two-month window to complete physical verification of every wetland or water body mapped in the SAC Atlas and place compliance reports before the court.
The litigation concerns wetlands identified by the Space Applications Centre under ISRO’s Wetland Atlas. Earlier proceedings revealed that the number of wetlands larger than 2.25 hectares had risen from 201,503 in earlier inventories to 231,195 in the 2021 SAC Atlas, making physical verification essential before legal protection could be extended.
In August 2025, the court had expressed dissatisfaction over the pace of compliance after a status report filed by the Union government showed several states had made little progress in ground-truthing and boundary demarcation. Calling the progress “snail’s pace”, it had granted another two months while cautioning that environment secretaries of defaulting states would have to personally appear before the court if the exercise remained incomplete. It had also directed states to publish details of identified wetlands, completed ground-truthing and boundary demarcation on their official websites and asked the Centre to coordinate with states for expeditious issuance of wetland notifications.
Also read: Man vs wild need not be our conservation model: Tech, financial stability in focus
The court had further clarified in October 2025 that the process of ground-truthing and demarcation must strictly comply with Rule 7 of the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 after concerns were raised that some authorities were carrying out demarcation before undertaking physical verification.
Apart from strengthening compliance directions, the bench also reappointed advocate Shibani Ghosh as nodal counsel to coordinate pleadings among all parties, state governments and wetland authorities in view of the voluminous record generated in the long-pending proceedings.
Also read: Habitat loss key challenge in conservation: Yadav on Gloal Tiger Day
Court declines funding requests
The bench also dealt with several intervention applications filed by Balakrishnan, who appeared in person seeking court directions for restoration of over 1,000 kunds in Vrindavan and a nationwide riverbank waste management project.
While acknowledging that the causes sought to be espoused were “laudable” and “benevolent”, the court refused to direct release of ₹80 crore and ₹1.038 lakh crore, respectively, to the intervener, observing that such work falls within the domain of statutory authorities and state governments. It, however, said the concerns raised regarding the protection of water bodies and river ecosystems would be kept in view while passing final orders in the main matter.

headline: Bengaluru: Even as Bengaluru's real estate market continues to witness robust demand, approvals for key proposals such as development plans, change of land use (CLU), building plans as well as occupancy certificates, have virtually come to a standsti...
full_text: Bengaluru: Even as Bengaluru's real estate market continues to witness robust demand, approvals for key proposals such as development plans, change of land use (CLU), building plans as well as occupancy certificates, have virtually come to a standstill at the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) and the Urban Development Department (UDD), leaving the sector in a limbo. .Industry insiders say the issue is widespread and not confined to a handful of developers. .While building plan approvals and occupancy certificates are processed by the GBA, CLU applications require clearance from the UDD. Builders claimed delays have been reported both at the GBA and the UDD levels, possibly indicating lack of work allocations. .Real estate push? Families in Bengaluru may lose 45% land for partition.In contrast, the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) and the Bangalore Metropolitan Region Development Authority (BMRDA), which also process a significant number of real estate projects, continue to clear applications without major delays. .What's more, the backlog has not just affected the developers but also delayed project completions and the issuance of occupancy certificates (OCs). An occupancy certificate is essential for obtaining an e-khata and, eventually, for handing over the property to the buyer. .While some officials cite the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls as the reason, builders believe the delays are also linked to the recent changes in the government. ."The town planning department is accepting applications from builders, but not processing them. There has effectively been a freeze for the past two months. The delay is affecting us badly. Some of our projects are on hold, and there is no clarity on when approvals will come," a builder said, adding that homebuyers have been repeatedly following up as developers are unable to hand over occupancy certificates on time. .Several builders said that although the real estate market had witnessed a sharp rise in sales, approvals had slowed considerably.."There is utter confusion among town planning officials," another builder said. "From khata-related matters to building plan approvals, there are hundreds of pending issues. Earlier, applications were handled through a central office. Now, the responsibility has been split among five corporations and each appears to be following a different process." .Builders said the problems that began after the formation of the GBA, which assumed planning powers earlier vested with the BDA, have worsened in recent months. ."The BDA continues to function smoothly because it is familiar with the approval system, though approvals often come at a cost. The BMRDA is also functioning efficiently and at a much faster pace. In comparison, the GBA has been slow," a well-known builder said. .With airport plan, 'Kanakapura Bande' as CM, real-estate buzz grows in South Bengaluru.B N Girish, GBA's Additional Director of Town Planning, said the issue could be limited to a few projects. "If applicants have not submitted the required no-objection certificates (NOCs) or if there are deficiencies in their applications, approvals will naturally be delayed. It could be specific to certain cases," he said. .However, one of the builders quoted earlier rejected that explanation, saying the problem is widespread and has already been taken up with the Confederation of Real Estate Developers' Associations of India (CREDAI). "We are told no meeting on approving CLUs has been held in the last two months. There is also a freeze on other town planning matters.".A developer said "There is utter confusion among town planning officials. Earlier applications were handled through a central office. Now the responsibility has been split among five corporations and each appears to be following a different process."

headline: A bead of sweat snakes down 44-year-old Rupesh Patil’s creased forehead as he scans a government notification. His restless gaze shifts abruptly from the still waters of Chirner Lake to the pastoral horizon of the historic village. The lake is near M...
full_text:
A bead of sweat snakes down 44-year-old Rupesh Patil’s creased forehead as he scans a government notification. His restless gaze shifts abruptly from the still waters of Chirner Lake to the pastoral horizon of the historic village. The lake is near Maharashtra’s 17th-Century Maha Ganpati Temple, and the area is known for its gadhegals — two ancient stones representing land-grant.
Chirner is among the 124 villages on the outskirts of Maharashtra’s capital, earmarked for the Third Mumbai project. “Ha navin prayatna ahe amchya jameeni hadapnyacha ani udyaogpatinchya ghashyat ghalnyacha. Kay garaj ahe, jameen ghenya aiwaji development karana. Malki amchich rahudya [This is the third attempt at grabbing all our lands at low prices and putting them in the laps of big conglomerates, contractors, and agents, who are manipulating farmers to sell],” says Patil.
He re-examines Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA)’s notification from October 2024. It announces the appointment of the New Town Development Authority (NTDA) as the Third Mumbai project’s special planning authority. The 323-square-kilometre project, also known as Karnala-Sai-Chirner Navanagar (KSC New Town project), is spread across Pen, Panvel, and Uran talukas (or tehsils) of Raigad district.
Chirner falls in the Uran taluka. On June 7, hundreds of people gathered in the village to protest, raising slogans to amplify their demand for fair compensation. Three days earlier, the Maharashtra Government had approved the appointment of Singapore-government-owned urban planning consultancy Surbana Jurong Group to prepare a master plan for Mumbai 3.0.
The villagers affected by the potential land acquisition are banded together in MMRDA KSC Navnagar Virodhi Samiti, a resistance group formed in April 2025. Their worry has roots in what they say is the Maharashtra government’s four-decade pattern of expanding Mumbai’s urban territory. The government, however, hails the Third Mumbai project as the next frontier of urban expansion.
Opposing expectations
The villagers want to ensure that their agricultural land is not acquired for a fraction of its worth. The government is offering the ready-reckoner rate, used to calculate property registration and stamp duty. The people of Raigad want the market rate, citing the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR Act).
Atul Mhatre, an architect from Dadargaon (or Dadar) in the Pen taluka of Raigad, is one of hundreds who will be affected. He owns three acres of land. “As per the ready reckoner, I will get ₹1 lakh per gunta, which, as per market price, is ₹5 lakh per gunta.” In Maharashtra, 40 guntas make one acre.
Expected to drive rapid urban growth, the Third Mumbai Project aims to decongest nearly 45% of the State’s urban population concentrated in the 4,312-square-kilometre tract of Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR). It comprises Mumbai City district, the Mumbai Suburban district area of the Konkan Division, and parts of Thane and Raigad. According to MMRDA’s Final Regional Plan for the Mumbai Metropolitan Region 2016–36, urban areas accounted for 62% of Maharashtra’s population growth in 2025.
Estimated at ₹4,000 crore, the Third Mumbai project sits within a 20-kilometre radius of three major economic gateways. With direct road access to South Mumbai, it is about 10-15 kilometres from Atal Setu (Mumbai Trans Harbour Link), 15-20 kilometres from Navi Mumbai International Airport, and 12-18 kilometres from Jawaharlal Nehru Port.
Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos this January, “Third Mumbai is an opportunity to create urban agglomeration; it has 60% data centre capacity. It will be a hub for new technology-enabling growth engines. With connectivity, it will bring Mumbai closer.” He said they plan to launch an Orange Gate tunnel, so people from Marine Drive, in the city centre, will be able to reach Navi Mumbai International Airport within 30 minutes. Once the Sewri–Worli Elevated Connector opens, those from the western suburbs can reach the airport in 30-45 minutes. “We are building connectivity. We can create a huge city, like Dubai, here. We have assessed the growth potential of MMR. It can alone become a 1.5 trillion economy.”
Priced possession
Nearly 60 metres from Chirner Lake, 28-year-old Amey Pitale walks briskly towards the Maha Ganpati Temple and sits on the steps. From his file, he pulls out a dog-eared notification issued by Maharashtra’s Urban Development department in 2019. It outlines the changed boundaries of MMR, extended to the 3 talukas of Raigad. Mr. Pitale’s father owns 2 acres of land, which is likely to be acquired under the project. “We are not against development if it is for us, the people of this land. MMR region, including Raigad, has a history of development at the cost of locals,” he says.
Three months before roping in Surbana Jurong to plan the Third Mumbai Project’s first phase, valued roughly at ₹11.89 crore, the Maharashtra government passed a resolution. It offered 3 provisions under which farmers could opt for compensation: land acquisition through mutual consent under Section 126(1)(a) of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966; compensation in lieu of cash in the form of Floor Space Index (FSI) or Transferable Development Rights (TDR); or allotment of 22.5% developed land as compensation for land acquisition.
MMRDA Commissioner Sanjay Mukherjee says, “The authority has given multiple choices for compensation, including the compensation under the 2013 Act.”
Another villager, Nilesh Patil, 40, joins Mr. Pitale at the temple. A chartered accountant, Mr. Patil has been keeping track of the infrastructure projects in Navi Mumbai. “Why does the government only believe in acquiring land? Why not bring on farmers as partners in the project?” he asks.
He also alleges that of the 22.5% of developed land, the farmers will receive only around 16% of the land parcel, as the rest is reserved for schools, hospitals, and community centres. “When and where [these buildings will be constructed] remains unanswered. Once the RFCTLARR Act is applied, farmers who are dissatisfied with the compensation or rehabilitation file a case in the court, which takes 10 years or so to be resolved. This has been their modus operandi,” Mr. Patil says.
Trust issues
The trust deficit pertaining to the Third Mumbai Project took root in April 2024, when MMRDA began consultations with Raigad residents. Farmers say they submitted 17,171 objections in an appeal. These pertained to land acquisition, compensation, and infrastructure development. However, according to a document from the Konkan Division’s Town Planning and Valuation Department, the MMRDA forwarded only 42 objections to the Urban Development Department (UDD) in September 2024.
On December 20, the MMRDA Virodhi Bhumiputra Sangarsh Samiti from Pen appealed to the UDD, alleging that most objections had been ignored.
During the Maharashtra Assembly’s winter session, the group burnt a copy of the appeal outside the Pen Provincial Administrator’s office. Social and political activist Nanda Mhatre cited the Maharashtra LARR (Amendment) Rules, 2023, questioning why no Social Impact Assessment (SIA) had been conducted to assess the impact on people, livelihoods, and communities.
In another letter dated April 22, 2026, responding to the March 16 Government Resolution on compensation, the farmers’ collective argued that the online consent form for land acquisition was vulnerable to fraudulent submissions and demanded that the process be halted until a transparent Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) was issued.
Responding to objections, MMRDA said the Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu) would spur regional development, justifying a new city in the public interest. On objections citing past experiences, it said these did not concern NTDA’s appointment.
Ms. Mhatre says, “We have objected to the entire project; NTDA is part of it. Did they take a hearing? No.”
MMRDA’s Mukherjee says, “The hearing is not required as written objections were taken and they have been responded to adequately.”
Past forward
The mention of urban development brings to the people’s mind the earliest memories of expansion and the angst of landowners who say they lost their farms to successive urban development projects.
The Navi Mumbai–Raigad region’s transformation began in 1970 when the City and Industrial Development Corporation (CIDCO) of Maharashtra was set up to decongest Mumbai. In the 70s, it acquired land from 95 villages, triggering protests led by farmer leader Dinkar Balu Patil. Acquisitions continued through the 1980s, including for Uran’s Dronagiri node, while Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority was commissioned in 1989.
In the early 2000s, the Navi Mumbai Special Economic Zone proposed acquiring land across 45 villages, but the idea was scrapped after a five-year agitation led by Ulka Mahajan and a referendum in 22 villages, where all 6,151 voters opposed it. In 2011, CIDCO acquired 1,160 hectares across 10 villages for the Navi Mumbai International Airport.
Once a farmer cultivating lentils, vegetables, and paddy on his half-acre farm, 54-year-old Jitendra Patil of Bokadvira village now works as a security guard earning ₹21,000 a month. He is forced to take on odd jobs. His land was acquired under CIDCO’s 1986 Navi Mumbai project for the Dronagiri node in Uran taluka. “I received ₹35,000 for 20 guntas. The District Court (Raigad-Alibag) later ordered CIDCO to pay about ₹55.9 lakh, but it is yet to do so. My family has grown, yet I cannot even build a room. Had I kept my farm, I could have survived and saved for the future,” he says.
Narrating a similar ordeal, 60-year-old Pramod Thakur recalls a 42-year legal battle initiated by his father. CIDCO acquired his 1.3-acre land in Uran in 1984 at ₹8 per square metre (about ₹43,000). Last year, the court ordered CIDCO to pay ₹850 per square metre (around ₹80 lakh). “I spent 40 years of my life to get my money; CIDCO is yet to pay the amount,” he says.
It’s been 20 years since Janga Bai, a 65-year-old woman from Mothi Jui village has been waiting for her land acquired under NMSEZ to be returned. At the gathering, she talks about the 12 guntas she gave for ₹5 lakh. “I was desperate for money because my husband needed medical care,” she says, which forced her to sell quickly.
Meanwhile, MMRDA has opened its portal for landowners to submit consent forms and supporting documents for acquisition by the NTDA. But Rupesh and the members of the MMRDA KSC Navnagar Virodhi Samiti say they have no intention of giving in.
“Raigad and Chirner have a legacy of satyagraha,” Rupesh says. It is a legacy the village wears with pride. On September 25, 1930, Chirner became the site of the Jungle Satyagraha, when hundreds of villagers defied British forest laws by entering the forests to collect firewood. The colonial police opened fire, killing 8 satyagrahis. The legal battle that followed was fought by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
Nearly a century later, the fight for many in Chirner is once again about land, rights, and dignity. “We will keep fighting,” Rupesh adds.

Prashant Kishor celebrates after winning the Bankipur Assembly bypoll (Image credit: PTI)
NEW DELHI: Jan Suraaj Party (JSP) founder Prashant Kishor has finally found a seat for his âschool bagâ in Bihar. The election strategist-turned-politician, whose party contests on a school bag symbol, has flipped the Bankipur assembly seat, an unassailable bastion of the BJP for the last 30 years. Before todayâs shock defeat, the BJP had registered 8 consecutive victories in Bankipur since 1995, when it won the seat for the first time.By-election in Bankipur was necessitated after Nitin Nabin resigned as BJP MLA from the seat in April after his election to Rajya Sabha. This followed Nitin Nabinâs elevation as BJP national president in January this year.To gauge the enormity of Prashant Kishorâs victory, look at these facts:
BJP has held Bankipur assembly seat from 1995 (Till 2005, the seat was known as Patna West)
BJP chief Nitin Nabin won from the Bankipur assembly seat four times in a row
Nitin Nabin won from Bankipur for first time in 2010 with a margin of 56%
From 1995 to 2010, the seat (known as Patna West) was represented by Navin Kishore Prasad Sinha (Nitin Nabinâs father)
Father-son duo has won the seat 8 consecutive times
For PK, as Prashant Kishor is popularly known, contesting the Bankipur byelection was a huge political gamble. PK, who made a high-pitched entry into Bihar politics with a padyatra spanning months ahead of the 2025 assembly elections, cut a sorry figure when his Jan Suraj Party failed to win even one seat less than a year ago. Such dismal was his first electoral show that JSP lost deposit in 236 of the 238 seats it contested. Prashant Kishor did not contest the election himself and instead led a high-voltage campaign for his party across the state.
Little wonder his decision to contest the Bankipur bypoll was fraught with the danger of becoming a make-or-break political move. But the gamble has paid off and Prashant Kishor with his debut win has propelled into the centrestage of Bihar politics.
âBankipurâs message to BJP central leadershipâ
Prashant Kishor polled over 64,151 votes and won the key electoral battle by a margin of 19,324 votes over BJPâs Neeraj Kumar. Prashant Kishorâs resounding success, nine months after his partyâs humiliating defeat, marks a remarkable turnaround.And making the most of his victory, Prashant Kishor immediately trained his guns at Bihar chief minister Samrat Choudhary."This is the victory of the people of Bankipur. As we stated during the election campaign, this was not just an election to choose an MLA. It was an attempt by the people of Bihar to send a message to the BJP's central leadership that they should appoint a good person as the chief minister of Bihar. They do not want a person with a criminal background or questionable conduct, character, or reputation to lead Bihar. They want a good chief minister who can improve education, create employment opportunities for the youth, and ensure that the children of Bihar do not have to migrate elsewhere for work," Kishor told reporters as his supporters celebrated his maiden electoral victory.
Prashant Kishor hits out at Bihar CM
Prashant Kishorâs use of his victory to target Samrat Choudhary did not come as a surprise. Ksihor been unrelenting in his attacks against the BJP leader ever since the election strategist became a full-time politician. He has targeted Samrat Choudhary over the chief ministerâs educational qualification and his alleged criminal past.
Kishor's development pitch or disappointment against BJP?
The Jan Suraaj chief also called upon the BJP's central leadership to focus on governance ahead of the next Lok Sabha elections, stating, "Before the Lok Sabha elections, Prime Minister Modi, the BJP, and Amit Shah should focus on improving Bihar, creating jobs for its youth, and stopping migration. That is our only objective. We do not want to become MLAs merely to award contracts. Our sole objective is the development of Bihar."These are the very themes on which Prashant Kishor fought the 2025 assembly elections and lost. Clearly, while he keeps focus on these issues, his victory in bankipur may less be about endorsement of his development focus and more about peopleâs disappointment with the BJP. The result is also perhaps a fallout of the studentsâ agitation against NEET-UG paper leak, which saw huge protests in Bihar. In Siwan, a police constable was suspended after a video purportedly showing him using an AK-47 rifle during a student protest on July 25 went viral on social media.Leader of opposition in Bihar assembly, Tejashwi Yadav, slammed Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary for the incident. He posted a video of the purported incident on X and, along with it, said, "During the protest in Siwan, police resorted to direct firing with an AK-47 on students. When a criminal becomes chief minister, then police fire bullets at innocent students.â
âVerdict by Bihar's youth against BJPâ
CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya in his message to Prashant Kishor described his victory as a significant verdict by Bihar's youth against the BJP-led state government.In a post on X, Bhattacharya termed Kishor's victory a "well-earned debut victory" and said the bypoll result reflected public anger against the ruling dispensation."Congratulations to Prashant Kishor on his well-earned debut victory in Bankipur bypoll. Kudos to the youth of Bihar for delivering such a telling blow to the supremely arrogant, incompetent and tyrannical BJP government of Bihar," he said.
Shock verdict for BJP
The BJP was quick to accept the verdict of the people. State BJP president Sanjay Saraogi said in a statement, "We bow before the will of the people. We shall draw lessons from the debacle, unlike our opponents who tend to blame every electoral loss of theirs on EVMs and the Election Commission".But for the BJP, this defeat comes as an embarrassment for both its national president Nitin Nabin and the partyâs first chief minister in the state Samrat Choudhary. Bankipur seat was literally a personal fiefdom of Nitin Nabinâs family which represented the constituency for 30 long years. A defeat in the backyard will surely embarrass the BJP chief.For Samrat Choudhary, this was the first electoral test of his government which was formed after the BJP took over the reins of the state from JD(U) chief Nitish Kumar. It was Nitish Kumar who had led the NDA to an emphatic triumph in the 2025 assembly elections. And the BJP would have hoped that Samrat Choudhary would have given it a winning start. But that was not to be.
Lalu's RJD pushed to fringes
The Bankipur bypoll result also has a worrying message for the main opposition party RJD. Tejashwi Yadavâs party seems to have learnt no lessons from the 2025 electoral drubbing. The party which has been reduced to 25 seats in the assembly did little to show intent on the ground.
Its candidate Rekha Kumari polled just 14,273 votes. This was over 32,000 votes less than the figure of 46,363, which she had polled in the 2025 assembly elections as the runnerup in the seat. Ironically, for the greater part of the campaign, RJDâs star campaigner Tejashwi Yadav was missing in action.
Time to pause, review
It may not be prudent to overexaggerate the outcome of one bypoll. The result of one seat, even though high-profile, may not be indicative of any larger trend. But for the BJP and the RJD to brush aside the defeat as a one-off setback would be doing harm to their cause. The BJP should remember that it rules Bihar but is still dependent on its allies for survival. The RJD, meanwhile, remains the main opposition party but seems to have lost the plot to factionalism and family feuds after its dismal 2025 show. Both need to pause and review what went wrong in Bankipur. MLA Prashant Kishor, on the other hand, will perhaps be now preparing for another bout with his political bete noir Samrat Choudhary - this time on the floor of Bihar assembly.
